basis: Independent source review and every current skill/step, including setup, teaching, criterion, easier option, dependencies and claim scope. Exact sequences are editorial adaptations, not clinically validated protocols.

LEAVE.title: Leave an item alone
LEAVE.goal: Turn away from a protected harmless item, on a cue or by a reinforced choice in practiced situations.
LEAVE.setup: Harmless low-interest practice items secured out of reach, better rewards and room to move away. For guarding, use individual professional help rather than approach-and-remove exercises.

steps.title: Reward turning away
steps.teach: Place a harmless low-interest item where the dog can see but cannot reach it. Begin far enough away for an easy brief look away. Mark that look away and promptly feed away from the item. Reset with space or a break. If attention sticks, increase distance or use a less interesting item; do not wait through frustration or provoke guarding.
steps.advance: Readily turns away from the protected item for a reward in 4 of 5 easy opportunities.
steps.easier: Make the item less interesting or start farther away; shorten the waiting time.
steps.setup: Secure a boring, harmless item behind a barrier or sturdy transparent cover that cannot be knocked aside. Begin far enough away for easy disengagement, with better rewards beside you and away from the item.

steps.title: Name the familiar turn away
steps.teach: Say “leave” once just before the familiar turn-away opportunity. Mark the turn and promptly reward from you, away from the item. Use one harmless floor item behind a secure barrier or under a sturdy clear cover. Fade your gesture before varying the item. Keep protection in place; never pull the dog away or test with hazards. This cue is useful communication, not a guarantee when you are absent.
steps.advance: Turns away on one cue from the selected safe floor item on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Increase distance or reduce item interest. Keep food, medicines, rubbish and other hazards inaccessible, including whenever nobody is supervising.
steps.setup: Prepare one harmless practice item under a sturdy clear cover or behind a secure barrier. Keep the floor clear, better rewards with you and enough distance for an easy turn; protection stays in place.

steps.title: Reward offered choices in another easy setup
steps.teach: Return to the easiest protected item. Without saying “leave,” mark a spontaneous look or step away and reward away from it. On another short practice, change only the harmless item OR its location and make the distance easier again. Mix these offered choices with separate familiar cued turns. Invited food-search games remain separate activities; this is not a rule that all food on the floor must be ignored.
steps.advance: Offers easy disengagement with more than one harmless protected item or placement across separate short practices; no prolonged staring or frustration.
steps.easier: Return to the original item and greater distance. If unprompted disengagement is not easy, help by ending the view rather than repeating tests.
steps.setup: Prepare a familiar protected harmless item and one similarly boring alternative. Keep both inaccessible and present only one at a time; set rewards away from the item and leave room to retreat.

steps.title: Try a little distance while you stay present
steps.teach: With the easiest protected setup, stand half a step farther away while remaining in the room and able to supervise. Reward an easy offered turn or use the familiar cue and reward that response. Record which occurred. Return closer between attempts. Change only handler distance; do not add absence, accessible hazards or more tempting items. Put items safely away after practice.
steps.advance: Comfortably disengages at the selected small handler distance in separate short practices; records distinguish cued responses from offered choices.
steps.easier: Return beside the dog or make the item less interesting. For times you cannot supervise, use secure storage and barriers rather than an unattended training test.
steps.setup: Use the familiar secured harmless item in a clear room with better rewards ready. Choose a tiny increase in your distance that still permits active supervision; nobody leaves the room.

WAIT.title: Short wait at an indoor doorway
WAIT.goal: Pause briefly before moving through a doorway together.
WAIT.setup: An interior door, open floor space, and no escape to outdoors.

steps.title: Reward a pause beside the doorway
steps.teach: At an open interior doorway, reward your dog for standing or sitting beside you for one second. Say “free” and move through together. Repeat until the pause is easy. Teach this beside a harmless doorway before involving an exterior door. As this becomes familiar, reward a pause the dog offers when you approach together, then release through the safe interior doorway. Do not require a fixed posture.
steps.advance: Offers a one-second pause with you in 4 of 5 easy repetitions.
steps.easier: Move farther from the doorway and shorten the pause. Avoid blocking the dog with your body.
steps.setup: Choose an open interior doorway with no access to outdoors. Clear the floor on both sides, keep the door still, and stand beside your dog with rewards within reach.

steps.title: Add gentle door movement
steps.teach: Say “wait,” move the interior door only an inch, and reward the pause before releasing. Build opening width in small changes, keeping the pause short. If your dog moves, calmly reset farther back and use a smaller door movement; never swing it into them. Keep waiting time short while changing opening width. A learned pause does not replace physical security at exits.
steps.advance: Can pause for a gentle full opening, then pass on release on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Use a smaller opening or no door movement. Continue using a leash/barrier at exterior doors regardless of training.
steps.setup: Use the familiar interior doorway, clear of paws and tails throughout the door's swing. Stand with your dog safely back from the edge and keep rewards available; no exterior exit should be exposed.

TOILET.title: Toilet routine
TOILET.goal: Use a predictable comfortable toilet location and tell you when needed.
TOILET.cue: Choose a toilet cue if useful
TOILET.setup: Regular access; investigate new accidents medically.

steps.title: Reward the right location
steps.teach: Offer a quiet toilet opportunity after waking, eating, play, and whenever your dog signals a need. Wait without pressuring them. As they finish in the chosen area, quietly reward there, then allow a little sniff time. Clean accidents without punishment.
steps.advance: A routine reliably creates successful opportunities; record the timing of any accidents to adjust access.
steps.easier: Offer more frequent easy access. Sudden accidents, straining, or increased drinking warrant a vet check.
steps.setup: Choose an accessible toilet spot and clear the route there. Keep outdoor clothing, a lead if needed, and rewards near the exit so trips after sleep, meals or play can be prompt.

steps.title: Add a cue and an easy request
steps.teach: Say your chosen toilet cue softly as elimination begins, then reward completion. If you want a request signal, reinforce a simple approach to the door by promptly offering a toilet trip; do not demand a long wait or a trick before access.
steps.advance: Uses the usual toilet area reliably with the planned routine; any request signal leads to a prompt opportunity.
steps.easier: Keep the schedule even if a request signal is not learned. Never delay access to test reliability.
steps.setup: Keep the familiar toilet route immediately accessible and rewards ready at the toilet spot. Choose the same cue in advance; any request signal must leave access to the door unobstructed.

FOODWAIT.title: Wait for a food-bowl invitation
FOODWAIT.goal: Pause briefly while a meal is placed and approach when invited.
FOODWAIT.setup: Use part of the normal meal and a quiet feeding area with one dog. Skip if food handling causes guarding or frustration; meals are never withheld for performance.

steps.title: A tiny pause before placement
steps.teach: Hold the bowl at a comfortable height while your dog stands freely nearby. Reward a moment with all paws on the floor, say “eat,” and place the bowl down within easy reach. Begin with almost no delay. Never repeatedly lift a bowl away as the dog approaches. This is optional bowl placement practice, not a condition for receiving meals. Feed promptly without a wait if it causes frustration; guarding calls for individual help, not bowl removal.
steps.advance: Comfortably pauses a moment and approaches the placed bowl after the invitation.
steps.easier: Feed the meal normally. Practice with a nearly empty bowl and a separate tiny reward another time.
steps.setup: Use the usual quiet feeding area with other animals separated. Put part of the normal meal in an easy-to-handle bowl and clear its landing spot. Skip waiting practice if bowl handling causes tension.

steps.title: Lower once, then invite
steps.teach: Say “wait” before lowering the bowl a small amount, reward that brief pause, then say “eat” as you finish placing it. Gradually lower farther before the invitation, keeping the pause only a second or two. If the dog moves early, simplify the next turn without taking food away.
steps.advance: Waits comfortably through one calm bowl placement and approaches on invitation in two mealtimes.
steps.easier: Use a smaller lowering movement or an immediate invitation. No long waits, hovering hands over food, or interference while eating.
steps.setup: Prepare the familiar bowl and clear feeding spot, with a separate small reward accessible. Stand at a comfortable lowering height with your dog free nearby; the meal remains available without a performance requirement.

ALONE.title: Very brief comfortable alone time
ALONE.goal: Practice small absences without distress; not a full panic-treatment program.
ALONE.setup: Camera; a familiar safe area; skip to individual help if absences already cause panic.

steps.title: Find an easy starting movement
steps.teach: With the camera positioned, begin while your dog is comfortably occupied or resting. Stand up or take one step away, then return before they worry. Observe posture, movement, and breathing, rather than requiring a stay. Repeat only a few easy movements with breaks.
steps.advance: Can make that small movement repeatedly without vigilance, following in distress, or other signs of worry.
steps.easier: Make the movement smaller or remain seated. For known separation panic, arrange professional support instead of testing their limit.
steps.setup: Place a camera where you can see your dog's whole body in their familiar safe area. Start while they are comfortably resting or occupied, with the floor around your chair clear. Do not test known separation panic.

steps.title: Try a moment out of view
steps.teach: Once moving within the room is easy, briefly lean beyond an interior doorway and return immediately. Watch the camera. Build tiny intervals below the onset of worry and mix easier repetitions into practice. Do not increase on every trial.
steps.advance: Several comfortable tiny absences in two sessions, with ordinary behavior throughout and after your return.
steps.easier: Reduce the absence to less than a second or return to in-view movements. Do not wait for crying to stop before returning.
steps.setup: Check that the camera shows your dog while you are briefly beyond a nearby interior doorway. Keep the return route clear, the door open and the starting distance within their established comfort.

steps.title: Make one departure action comfortable
steps.teach: Choose one departure action, such as touching keys. Start with a smaller or quieter version that your dog notices comfortably, then offer something they enjoy and remain at home. Repeat only a few easy times with breaks; do not rehearse worry. This can run alongside in-view movement practice. Tiny absences stay at the level comfortable in ALONE-2 and are combined with this action only after both are easy. Longer departures need an individual supported plan.
steps.advance: The selected departure action can occur without vigilance or distress across separate short practices. This does not certify any duration alone.
steps.easier: Choose a smaller action or put the prop away. Manage necessary absences to avoid distress while arranging individualized veterinary or qualified behavior support.
steps.setup: Keep your dog in their comfortable familiar area with a camera available to observe their whole body. Choose one quiet departure action and suitable rewards; this exercise includes no departure.

CROSS.title: Cross a quiet road together
CROSS.goal: Combine a curb pause with a short uninterrupted crossing at the handler’s invitation.
CROSS.setup: A quiet lawful crossing with clear sight lines, comfortable fitted equipment and a capable adult. Rehearse away from vehicles first.

steps.title: Rehearse the whole path indoors
steps.teach: Mark two harmless flat lines several steps apart. Pause at the first as in curb practice, say “cross,” and walk straight to the far line with your dog on a slack lead. Reward on the far side. Keep the middle free of sniff rewards so the destination is clear.
steps.advance: Completes pause, invitation and a few continuous steps to the far line comfortably.
steps.easier: Shorten the pretend crossing or practice loose steps separately. No leash pressure to keep pace.
steps.setup: Mark two harmless flat lines a few steps apart on a non-slip indoor floor. Clear the route between them, prepare rewards beyond the far line, and use a comfortable familiar lead setup.

steps.title: One quiet checked crossing
steps.teach: At a suitable real crossing, keep the dog safely back from the edge while you check all directions. When the route is clear, say “cross” and walk together to a safe spot beyond the far curb. Reward there. If anything changes, prioritize human safety decisions over the exercise.
steps.advance: Completes the short human-managed crossing without stopping in the roadway in two quiet outings.
steps.easier: Return to the pretend route or choose a quieter place. Never rehearse against active traffic or rely on the cue for safety.
steps.setup: Choose a quiet lawful crossing with clear sight lines and safe standing space beyond both curbs. A capable adult checks secure equipment and traffic; have rewards accessible for the far side.

DOG.title: Seeing a dog predicts good things
DOG.goal: Feel comfortable observing another dog from an individually suitable distance.
DOG.setup: Open space, clear exit, secure comfortable equipment; cooperative helper and calm adult dog if arranging practice.

steps.title: Find a comfortable viewing setup
steps.teach: Choose a wide quiet area where you can retreat without passing the other dog. Begin farther away than you think necessary. Allow one brief distant sighting, then leave the view. Record distance and body language without approaching to find the breaking point. Both dogs and handlers need to be comfortable. Promptly offer desired food when the helper is comfortably noticed; no obedience is needed. This is a brief supported observation, not a test of how long the dog can tolerate a view.
steps.advance: Can notice the helper dog with loose movement and ordinary interest, then return to baseline when the view ends.
steps.easier: Start farther away or use a partial visual barrier. If no comfortable setup is available, use management and individual professional help.
steps.setup: Agree with a capable helper on a calm adult dog, wide separation and a way to end the view. Check comfortable secure equipment and a retreat that does not pass the helper; start conservatively far away.

steps.title: Pair the sight with food
steps.teach: At the easy distance, let your dog notice the other dog; promptly feed several tiny desired treats. When the helper goes out of view, let the feeding pause. No sit, silence, or eye contact is required. Allow a break and repeat only after the dog has returned to baseline.
steps.advance: Across two sessions, several brief sightings stay comfortable and the dog begins relaxed food anticipation on seeing the helper.
steps.easier: Increase distance or shorten the glimpse. If a bark or startle occurs, help them leave and simplify; do not withhold food as punishment.
steps.setup: Use the recorded comfortable separation with the same helper and dog. Arrange brief views that the helper can end, keep desired food ready with you, and leave the retreat completely clear.

steps.title: Vary one easy feature
steps.teach: Keep the safe distance and have the helper take one slow step sideways, then stop. Pair the sight/movement with food as before. Mix still, easier sightings between moving ones. On a later day you may change distance slightly instead, while keeping movement easy.
steps.advance: Several comfortable observations in two sessions at this one new version, with recovery no slower than the easy baseline.
steps.easier: Remove the movement or return to the previous distance. Reduced distance is optional; comfortable coexistence is the goal.
steps.setup: Keep the successful distance, secure equipment and retreat unchanged. Agree that the helper will make only one small sideways movement on request; prepare rewards and an immediate way to end the view.

PARALLEL.title: Walk parallel at a comfortable distance
PARALLEL.goal: Move in the same direction as a helper dog without needing contact.
PARALLEL.setup: Two capable handlers, wide quiet space, no convergence; individualized help for aggression or redirection.

steps.title: Add parallel movement
steps.teach: After a comfortable stationary sighting, have both handlers walk in the same direction at the established wide separation. Keep the dogs from converging. Walk only a few steps, promptly offer desired food when the helper is noticed comfortably, with extra rewards for freely offered check-ins, then curve farther apart for a break.
steps.advance: Both dogs remain comfortable through several short parallel stretches and recover normally after breaks.
steps.easier: Increase separation and shorten the stretch, or return to stationary sightings. Do not walk directly toward each other.
steps.setup: Arrange two capable handlers on wide, separate walking lines in a quiet open area. Start at the established comfortable separation, check equipment, and agree on the same direction and outward break routes.

steps.title: Extend the easy stretch
steps.teach: Repeat short parallel stretches at the successful separation. Gradually lengthen only the walking portion, keeping direction and speed predictable. Give regular sniff breaks apart. Decrease separation on a separate day only if that is useful and both dogs remain comfortable.
steps.advance: Completes practical short parallel stretches in two sessions without tension building or recovery slowing.
steps.easier: Use shorter stretches or a wider route. This exercise does not require or imply readiness for a greeting.
steps.setup: Use the same successful separation, direction and calm helper dog. Choose a slightly longer clear stretch with separate sniff-break areas and ample room to widen apart without crossing paths.

VISITOR.title: Comfortable separated visitor routine
VISITOR.goal: Coexist with a visitor through a planned separated setup.
VISITOR.setup: Cooperative adult; trusted company if needed; secure barrier; no bite-risk exposure without professional support.

steps.title: Rehearse without a visitor
steps.teach: Practice moving your dog into their comfortable refuge before you touch the entry door. Give a suitable activity if enjoyed; someone may stay with them. Rehearse opening and closing the entryway while the dog stays safely separated and comfortable.
steps.advance: The whole no-visitor arrangement is comfortable on several rehearsals in two sessions.
steps.easier: Keep more trusted company, more distance, or an open interior view. Do not use confinement that causes panic.
steps.setup: Prepare the dog's already comfortable refuge, a secure barrier and a suitable familiar activity if enjoyed. Arrange trusted company if needed and clear your route to the entry; no visitor is present.

steps.title: Bring in one quiet adult while separated
steps.teach: Arrange a no-knock arrival. Settle your dog in the refuge first, then admit the cooperative adult, who sits quietly away from it. Stay with or monitor the dog. Pair any noticed mild arrival sounds with desired rewards; end the visit before distress develops.
steps.advance: Dog remains comfortable through several short quiet separated visits; duration and any sounds are recorded.
steps.easier: Shorten the visit, increase sound insulation or distance, or keep the adult outside. Greeting is unnecessary.
steps.setup: Arrange one cooperative adult for a no-knock arrival and a quiet seat away from the refuge. Secure your dog in the familiar comfortable arrangement first, with monitoring or trusted company and rewards ready.

steps.title: Offer an optional distant view
steps.teach: Only if safe and your dog is comfortable with STRANGER practice, offer a brief distant view of the seated adult through a secure barrier. You supply food; the adult ignores the dog. End the view while comfortable and return to the refuge. Staying fully separated is also a successful long-term option.
steps.advance: Several optional views are comfortable with easy retreat and normal recovery across two visits.
steps.easier: Skip the view or shorten it. A dog that approaches for food has not necessarily invited touch.
steps.setup: Only use an established safe separated arrangement and comfortable STRANGER starting distance. Seat the adult behind a secure barrier, keep your own rewards ready, and ensure you can end the view immediately.

steps.title: Add one visitor action
steps.teach: At the successful fully separated arrangement, ask the seated adult to say one quiet word, then stop; pair the noticed sound promptly with desired food. No view is required. If you choose visible movements, first use the safe comfortable viewing setup in VISITOR-3. Change only one action per practice and keep the barrier and retreat. Rebuild with each new person.
steps.advance: Comfortable observations of the selected action over two visits; no pressure to approach or remove the barrier.
steps.easier: Use a smaller action, greater separation, or no view. Escalation or bite concerns require an individual plan.
steps.setup: Recreate the successful separated or viewing arrangement with the same adult and secure barrier. Agree on one quiet word or small movement and a stop signal, with your rewards and retreat ready.

SOUND.title: Controlled sound practice
SOUND.goal: Build a positive association with one adjustable sound.
SOUND.setup: One chosen sound; controllable speaker; quiet home; stop playback immediately if needed.

steps.title: Find a faint noticeable version
steps.teach: Choose just one sound and record the starting volume/speaker position. Play a split-second faint version from a distance. If it is noticed comfortably, promptly offer desired food. End playback and allow a break. Do not loop a track while waiting for the dog to stop reacting.
steps.advance: Several noticeable faint presentations stay comfortable across two sessions.
steps.easier: Reduce volume, shorten the clip, or move the speaker farther away. No reaction to a recording may mean it is not meaningful to this dog.
steps.setup: Choose one brief sound clip in a quiet home and a player with an immediate stop control. Set a faint volume and distant speaker position, note both settings, and keep desired food ready.

steps.title: Change one sound feature
steps.teach: Repeat the successful sound–food pairing. Make only one small change: slightly longer OR slightly louder, while all else stays easy. Include easier trials. Stop the sound and simplify if posture tightens, scanning increases, or recovery takes longer.
steps.advance: Comfortable observations at the selected new setting in two sessions, with ordinary recovery between them.
steps.easier: Return to the original setting or choose a more controllable sound; do not increase until the dog reacts.
steps.setup: Recreate the successful recording, speaker position and volume. Decide on one tiny duration or volume change before starting, with an immediate stop control and rewards within reach.

steps.title: Try a modest realistic variation
steps.teach: Keep the session easy while changing just the sound source or location slightly, such as the same recording played farther from another doorway. Rebuild from the quiet version. Real outdoor events and storms require their own management and cannot be certified safe by recording progress.
steps.advance: The specific realistic variation is comfortable across two sessions; separate limits for real events are written down.
steps.easier: Return to the familiar source or environment. Avoid formal training during an already frightening noise event.
steps.setup: Choose one modest source or location variation and reset playback to an easy quiet level. Keep the dog's familiar retreat open, rewards ready, and real frightening noise events outside this practice.

STORM.title: Prepare for unavoidable noise events
STORM.goal: Use a practiced refuge and support plan during storms or fireworks.
STORM.setup: Discuss severe noise fear with your vet before the event; this is a management plan.

steps.title: Rehearse the support arrangement
steps.teach: On a quiet day, set up a quiet refuge with familiar bedding, close curtains, check escape routes, and try gentle masking sound if your dog likes it. Sit nearby and let them choose to hide, rest, or seek contact. Rehearse any veterinarian-prescribed plan only as directed by that veterinarian.
steps.advance: The refuge, trusted company, and any ordinary sound masking are familiar and comfortable before the event.
steps.easier: Remove masking that worries the dog or change the resting location. A crate is suitable only if already comfortable.
steps.setup: Choose a quiet day to prepare familiar bedding, curtains and secure exits in the refuge. Have water and trusted company available; use masking sound only if already comfortable and follow any veterinary plan as prescribed.

steps.title: Prepare to use and review the plan
steps.teach: On a quiet day, write when you will bring your dog inside, secure exits and prepare the familiar refuge. Check that trusted support and any veterinarian-prescribed plan are available. During an actual event, offer food, play or contact if wanted without requiring a posture. Afterward record comfort and recovery and review poor outcomes with your vet before the next event. Do not create a noise event to complete this step.
steps.advance: The practical support plan is written and ready. Review it after real events when they occur; completing this step does not mean noise fear is cured.
steps.easier: Increase protection and trusted support; do not test louder exposure. Panic or persistent distress calls for veterinary reassessment.
steps.setup: On a quiet day, have your refuge checklist, support contacts and any existing veterinary instructions ready. Rehearse ordinary preparations without noise exposure; no storm or fireworks event is needed.

OBJECT.title: Comfort with an object or appliance
OBJECT.goal: Handle a gradual, voluntary introduction to one specific object.
OBJECT.setup: Object off and stationary first; dog can leave without crossing its path.

steps.title: Start with the object still and off
steps.teach: Place the stationary switched-off object far enough away for your dog to notice comfortably. Promptly offer desired food from you when it is noticed; no approach or posture is required. Let the dog retreat. If sight alone is worrying, use more distance or a partial view. Do not lure toward the object or withhold support while waiting for exploration.
steps.advance: Several brief comfortable views across two sessions; the dog can choose ordinary movement and retreat.
steps.easier: Increase distance or show less of the object. Do not place food on it to force approach.
steps.setup: Place the object switched off and stable at a generous distance. Keep your dog's route away clear without crossing its path, have rewards with you, and screen part of the view if needed.

steps.title: Add a tiny movement
steps.teach: At the comfortable distance, have a helper move the object an inch, then stop; immediately provide desired food. For a vacuum, keep it switched off here. Repeat only after baseline returns and keep the dog’s escape path clear.
steps.advance: The selected tiny movement is comfortable in multiple observations over two sessions.
steps.easier: Use a smaller movement or a more distant helper; remove motion if posture tightens.
steps.setup: Keep the object switched off at its established comfortable distance. Arrange a helper for one tiny movement and an immediate stop, with your dog's exit clear and food ready beside you.

steps.title: Introduce sound separately
steps.teach: Begin with a very faint brief recording or a helper running the appliance behind a distant closed door, while the dog has a clear retreat. Pair the comfortably noticed sound promptly with desired food, then stop. No visible object or movement is needed. Rebuild sound and visible movement separately; only after each is comfortable should any combination begin at an easier level.
steps.advance: Several brief sound-only presentations remain comfortable in separate short practices, with ordinary behavior and recovery. Combining sound and movement is not required.
steps.easier: Return to one component only or arrange for the dog to stay elsewhere during actual use.
steps.setup: Prepare a faint recording or a helper controlling the appliance behind a distant closed door. Keep the dog in a comfortable separate area with rewards and an immediate sound cutoff; do not add visible motion yet.

ELEVATOR.title: Ride a quiet elevator comfortably
ELEVATOR.goal: Choose entry and a short attended elevator ride with comfortable exits.
ELEVATOR.setup: Use a quiet authorized elevator with a helper, non-slip footing and enough room. Keep dogs and equipment clear of door tracks; humans control access and never use the dog to hold doors.

steps.title: Watch from a comfortable distance
steps.teach: Stay well outside the doorway and let the empty elevator open and close while you reward comfortable observation. Move away after each brief look. Begin far enough back that sounds and people do not trap the dog. Skip crowded times and let the dog choose to leave.
steps.advance: Comfortably observes a few quiet door cycles and approaches only by choice.
steps.easier: Use more distance or stop at a partial view. Take another route when possible.
steps.setup: Choose a quiet authorized elevator and a roomy viewing position well outside its doorway. Arrange a helper, secure comfortable equipment, rewards and an unobstructed retreat; avoid passenger traffic.

steps.title: Enter and exit while stationary
steps.teach: With a helper safely using the door controls according to building rules, invite a voluntary step into the stationary empty car. Reward and exit promptly together. Build toward a full brief entry with enough room to turn. Keep the lead slack and all feet clear of the moving-door zone. Use an ordinary short non-retractable leash with slack. Handler and dog enter and exit together; never let the doors separate them or close on the leash.
steps.advance: Chooses full entry and a calm immediate exit in several stationary rehearsals.
steps.easier: Reward approaching from outside. Never lure a worried dog past a closing door.
steps.setup: Arrange a helper to operate door controls according to building rules. Use an empty stationary car with non-slip footing, enough turning room and lead slack; keep all feet and equipment clear of the door tracks.

steps.title: One short quiet ride
steps.teach: After easy entries, choose a single short ride with a familiar adult beside the dog. Reward comfort as the doors close and the car moves, then leave together at the next safe opening. Keep other people out of the training plan and finish after one ride.
steps.advance: Comfortably completes a short ride and ordinary exit on two quiet occasions.
steps.easier: Return to stationary entry or use an alternative route. Motion distress, nausea or panic calls for individual support.
steps.setup: Plan one short quiet ride after comfortable entries. Have a familiar adult beside the dog, rewards ready and a clear exit at the destination; avoid crowds and keep the lead away from door tracks.

AUTODOOR.title: Pass through automatic doors
AUTODOOR.goal: Approach and walk through a wide automatic doorway without rushing or startling.
AUTODOOR.setup: A quiet permitted entrance with a helper, broad clearance and room to retreat. Humans verify the sensor and opening; avoid revolving doors.

steps.title: Watch the moving panels
steps.teach: Stand far enough to the side for an unobstructed view without triggering the doors yourself. Have a helper activate one cycle while you reward your dog for comfortable observation. Let them leave and return. Never put the dog in the opening to make the sensor respond.
steps.advance: Comfortably observes several predictable cycles with ordinary loose movement.
steps.easier: Watch from farther away or choose a quieter entrance. Motion comfort comes before passage.
steps.setup: Choose a quiet permitted entrance with a cooperative helper. Stand to one side outside the sensor area, with secure equipment, rewards and a broad retreat; the helper will activate the panels.

steps.title: One generous walking pass
steps.teach: Have the helper safely activate the doors and confirm they are fully open. Invite your dog to walk beside you through the broad opening, reward beyond it, then take a break. Keep the lead and tail clear and walk at a natural pace, with room to abort before entry. Use an ordinary short non-retractable leash with slack and pass through together. Never depend on the sensor detecting the dog or leash.
steps.advance: Walks through a fully open doorway comfortably in two short visits.
steps.easier: Return to observation or use a manual alternative. Never hurry a hesitant dog through narrowing panels.
steps.setup: Arrange the helper to activate the doors and verify a fully open, generous passage. Clear the approach and far-side reward area, check lead and tail clearance, and retain room to turn away before entry.

CHIN.title: Voluntary chin rest
CHIN.goal: Place the chin on a hand or towel without restraint.
CHIN.setup: Dog comfortable with hands near the face; no painful area handling.

steps.title: Capture chin placement
steps.teach: Hold an open palm or folded towel just below chin height, without pressing upward. Reward a voluntary approach, then a light chin contact. Toss a reset reward away and offer again. If a small lure is useful, fade it early; the dog chooses contact.
steps.advance: Offers a light chin contact repeatedly without a hand moving into the face.
steps.easier: Use a towel on a low support or reward a smaller approach. Get help if face handling worries the dog.
steps.setup: Sit beside your dog with an empty palm or folded towel just below natural chin height. Support any towel securely, keep rewards separate, and leave room to lift the head and move away.

steps.title: Add a short hold and an exit
steps.teach: Reward a half-second of voluntary chin contact, then invite a break. Build to one or two seconds with easier attempts mixed in. Add “chin” just before offering the familiar target. Lifting the chin ends the attempt; never hold it down or block withdrawal. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Offers and briefly holds the target on the chosen cue/signal in 4 of 5 comfortable attempts across two sessions.
steps.easier: Shorten the hold and reward sooner. This posture alone is not proof that handling feels safe.
steps.setup: Use the familiar chin target at the same comfortable height. Keep your supporting hand still, rewards readily available and the route away clear; do not plan additional handling during this step.

HANDLE.title: Cooperative gentle handling
HANDLE.goal: Participate in a tiny, non-painful care action with a clear stop option.
HANDLE.setup: Only healthy comfortable areas; veterinary direction for painful or urgent care.

steps.title: Make one small hand movement comfortable
steps.teach: With the dog free to leave, offer the known chin target. Move your other hand slightly toward a comfortable shoulder, then stop and reward. End hand movement immediately if the chin lifts. Wait for a voluntary new start; do not keep repositioning the dog. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Several small hand movements are comfortable and the handler consistently honors withdrawal.
steps.easier: Make the hand motion smaller or omit the chin signal until the dog is comfortable with the setup.
steps.setup: Choose a healthy comfortable shoulder area and sit beside your dog with the familiar chin target ready. Keep the other hand initially clear of the body and rewards within reach; urgent or painful care needs veterinary direction.

steps.title: Add a moment of gentle touch
steps.teach: After a voluntary start, touch the healthy shoulder lightly for less than a second, remove the hand, and reward. Build one feature at a time—brief duration OR a nearby body area—while continuing to stop at withdrawal. Do not use food to conceal a difficult procedure. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Several brief touches in two sessions are comfortable, with easy re-initiation and no avoidance after the break.
steps.easier: Use a shorter/lighter touch. Stop and consult the vet for new sensitivity or possible pain.
steps.setup: Prepare the same healthy shoulder area and freely offered chin target. Keep rewards accessible and your touching hand light and easy to withdraw; no restraint or hidden procedure is part of this turn.

BRUSH.title: Comfort with a brush or towel
BRUSH.goal: Accept a brief gentle grooming action voluntarily.
BRUSH.setup: Suitable gentle tool; skin healthy; dog can leave.

steps.title: Introduce the tool separately
steps.teach: Show a soft brush or towel at a comfortable distance, then reward. Put it away between presentations. After comfortable sighting, move it slightly near a healthy easy area without touching, reward, and remove. Do not begin with a tangle or a sensitive spot. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Comfortable with the tool’s appearance and small movement in several short sessions.
steps.easier: Use a softer tool or greater distance; ask your vet about skin discomfort.
steps.setup: Choose a soft suitable brush or towel and a quiet non-slip area. Keep the tool at a comfortable initial distance, rewards separate, and an open exit; avoid sore skin and tangled coat.

steps.title: Try one gentle stroke
steps.teach: After a voluntary start signal or relaxed approach, give one light short stroke on a comfortable shoulder, then stop and reward. Wait for the dog to choose another turn. Gradually try two strokes, mixing single easy ones in. End at any withdrawal. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Repeated short grooming turns are comfortable across two sessions, with no avoidance afterward.
steps.easier: Reduce pressure or use only a momentary towel touch. Painful matting or necessary grooming needs an individualized care plan.
steps.setup: Use the familiar soft tool and a healthy tangle-free shoulder area. Sit beside rather than over your dog, with rewards ready and their voluntary start or free approach available; do not hold them in place.

NAIL.title: Paw-care preparation
NAIL.goal: Be comfortable with tiny paw/tool preparations; clipping is a separate skilled procedure.
NAIL.setup: Non-slip surface; healthy paws; knowledgeable guidance before actual trimming.

steps.title: Start above the paw
steps.teach: With your dog free to stand or lie comfortably, briefly touch a healthy upper leg, remove the hand, and reward. Gradually work lower over separate sessions, stopping if the dog pulls away. Do not grab or hold a paw to prevent movement. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Light contact near the paw remains comfortable in several observations over two sessions.
steps.easier: Stay higher on the leg or use a shorter touch. New paw sensitivity needs veterinary assessment.
steps.setup: Provide a non-slip surface where your dog can comfortably stand or lie. Choose a healthy upper leg, keep rewards ready and your hands visible; sore or newly sensitive paws need veterinary assessment first.

steps.title: Separate tool appearance from contact
steps.teach: Show the nail tool at a comfortable distance, reward, and put it away. Introduce its quiet sound separately if relevant. Bring it slightly nearer only while the dog freely remains comfortable; stop well short of paw contact. Paw-touch preparation can run separately at NAIL-1. Actual clipping or grinding needs individual instruction on anatomy, technique and comfort, rather than following automatically. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Comfortable with the selected non-contact preparation in two sessions; an appropriate next-care plan is arranged.
steps.easier: Return the tool farther away or omit its sound. Never restrain the paw to finish a training repetition.
steps.setup: Prepare a nail tool for viewing only at a comfortable distance, with any sound controllable separately. Keep paws untouched, rewards ready and the dog free to leave; actual trimming requires individual instruction.

TEETH.title: Voluntary toothbrushing preparation
TEETH.goal: Build comfortable participation in gentle veterinary-guided mouth care.
TEETH.setup: Veterinary clearance for any dental pain; a demonstrated technique, pet-safe paste and soft suitable brush. No human toothpaste or forced jaw opening.

steps.title: Comfort with the care items
steps.teach: Let the dog see the soft brush at a comfortable distance and reward relaxed interest. Separately offer a tiny taste of veterinarian-approved pet toothpaste if suitable. Keep hands away from the mouth while building pleasant associations with the items. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Comfortably sees the brush and voluntarily accepts the chosen pet-safe taste if used.
steps.easier: Remove the paste, increase brush distance, or ask the veterinary team about discomfort or suitable materials.
steps.setup: Have a soft pet brush and veterinarian-approved pet toothpaste ready separately from rewards. Use a comfortable non-slip area and obtain veterinary advice for oral pain; no human toothpaste or mouth handling is needed here.

steps.title: Invite a tiny lip touch
steps.teach: Ask your veterinary team to demonstrate a suitable safe approach. When the dog voluntarily offers their familiar chin rest, briefly touch the outer lip area as demonstrated, remove your hand, and reward. Stop immediately if the dog withdraws. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Freely offers repeated start signals and stays comfortable with a momentary gentle lip-area touch.
steps.easier: Return to hand movement at a distance. Pain, guarding, or resistance calls for individual help, not holding the head.
steps.setup: First obtain a veterinary demonstration of a suitable outer-lip approach. Prepare the familiar chin target, clean hands and rewards beside your dog, with an open exit; do not proceed with pain or guarding concerns.

steps.title: One gentle outside-tooth stroke
steps.teach: Following the veterinary demonstration and only after comfortable lip-area work, use the soft pet brush for one gentle brief stroke on an accessible outer tooth surface. Stop, reward, and offer a break. Add tiny amounts of brushing only while participation remains voluntary. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Comfortably accepts one gentle demonstrated stroke and willingly returns for another invitation. Full brushing is built gradually with veterinary guidance.
steps.easier: Return to brush presence or lip-area work. Stop for pain, bleeding, tension, avoidance, or any need for restraint.
steps.setup: Following the veterinary demonstration, prepare the suitable soft pet brush and approved paste if appropriate. Use the familiar voluntary care position with rewards ready; no forced jaw opening or restraint is planned.

CLIP.title: Accept a leash clip
CLIP.goal: Voluntarily remain comfortable while a lead is clipped and unclipped.
CLIP.setup: Comfortable already-worn equipment, a quiet light clip and a freely accessible exit. Check fit separately; no reaching to grab the dog.

steps.title: Clip sound and hand approach
steps.teach: Hold the lead far enough away for comfort, operate the clip softly, then reward. Separately bring an empty hand a little toward the attachment point, reward and withdraw. Let the dog step away whenever wanted. Keep the sound and reach separate until both are easy. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Comfortable with the quiet clip sound and a short hand approach over several voluntary turns.
steps.easier: Muffle or replace a loud clip and increase distance. Do not touch equipment while the dog avoids you.
steps.setup: Start with comfortable already-worn equipment and your dog awake and free to leave. Have a quiet light clip, rewards and room for a visible hand approach; check equipment fit separately.

steps.title: Attach, reward, remove
steps.teach: Invite the dog near, briefly touch the familiar attachment area, reward and withdraw. After easy touches, attach the clip, reward, then remove it immediately. Keep the line supported so it does not swing into legs. Slowly add a few comfortable steps only when attachment itself is unremarkable. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Freely approaches for clipping and unclipping and moves comfortably afterward in two sessions.
steps.easier: Return to the hand approach or equipment comfort. Clipping is not permission to restrain a worried dog.
steps.setup: Use the familiar attachment point and clip in a quiet clear area. Support the loose lead so it cannot swing into legs, keep rewards accessible, and leave room for an immediate release and a few easy steps. Check comfort and fit before attaching the lead.

COLLAR.title: Comfortable collar contact
COLLAR.goal: Stay relaxed through a brief gentle human touch of the collar or harness attachment area.
COLLAR.setup: Well-fitted comfortable equipment and an awake willing dog. Touch only; no jerks, choking or surprise grabs. Useful for safe handling but not a test of restraint tolerance.

steps.title: Predict a brief touch
steps.teach: Say the chosen warning softly, reach only partway toward the equipment, reward and withdraw. Build toward a momentary finger contact on the outside without gripping. Keep your hand visible from the side, and let any movement away end the turn. Practice before a real need arises. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Voluntarily stays loose through several predicted brief outside touches.
steps.easier: Reach less far or use an easier body area. Skip and seek help for guarding or bite risk.
steps.setup: Choose a quiet moment with your dog awake and willing in familiar well-fitted equipment. Sit or stand to the side with visible hands, rewards ready and an open retreat; skip for guarding or bite risk.

steps.title: A loose momentary hold
steps.teach: After easy contact, briefly place fingers around a safe section of equipment with no pressure on the neck or body. Reward and release immediately. Mix contact-only turns with this tiny hold. Never use a treat to conceal a grab or keep holding until the dog stops resisting. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Freely returns for predicted momentary no-pressure holds across two easy sessions.
steps.easier: Return to a touch. This does not make grabbing, lifting by equipment or restraint during fear safe.
steps.setup: Use the successful comfortable side position and a safe reachable section of equipment. Keep rewards accessible and the lead slack, with room to release your fingers immediately without pressure on neck or body.

RINSE.title: Step into a shallow paw rinse
RINSE.goal: Voluntarily place feet in a broad shallow tray of plain water.
RINSE.setup: A broad stable non-slip tray, shallow lukewarm plain water, dry safe exits and healthy paws. No detergents or forced immersion; veterinary advice for skin problems.

steps.title: Explore the dry tray
steps.teach: Secure the broad tray so it cannot slide or wobble. Reward looking, approaching and voluntary foot contacts with the empty surface. Invite an easy step off after each contact. Build toward comfortable standing only if all feet fit with room; never place paws into the tray yourself. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Voluntarily steps into and out of the stable dry tray several times.
steps.easier: Use a flat non-slip mat or a wider tray. Stop at any uneven movement.
steps.setup: Secure a broad empty tray on a non-slip floor, with room for all feet and a dry easy exit. Check healthy paws and smooth edges; keep rewards with you and no water present.

steps.title: A trace of water
steps.teach: Add only enough plain water to dampen a small area while the dog is away. Let them inspect and reward a voluntary single foot contact, then offer an immediate exit. Increase coverage only across comfortable turns. Keep water still, without pouring or splashing near the dog. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Chooses to place feet on the wet surface and freely returns after a break.
steps.easier: Use less water or return to a dry tray. Do not hold a foot in place.
steps.setup: While your dog is away, dampen only a small part of the familiar secured tray with lukewarm plain water. Prepare a dry non-slip exit and rewards; avoid pouring or splashing near them. Use healthy paws only; follow veterinary advice for skin problems.

steps.title: A short rinse pause
steps.teach: Invite the familiar tray entry with the chosen cue. Reward a brief comfortable stand in very shallow water, then invite an exit onto a dry non-slip surface. Any later wiping is a separate invitation. Empty the tray after use rather than leaving standing water accessible. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Enters on invitation, pauses comfortably and exits in two short sessions.
steps.easier: Rinse one willing foot briefly or use another vet-advised cleaning method. Stop for skin irritation or discomfort.
steps.setup: Prepare very shallow lukewarm plain water in the familiar broad non-slip tray. Keep a dry secure exit ready, rewards accessible and supervision continuous; avoid detergents and follow veterinary advice for skin problems.

EAR.title: Offer an outer-ear check
EAR.goal: Voluntarily participate in a tiny visual check of a healthy outer ear.
EAR.setup: Healthy pain-free ears, clean hands and a known chin start signal. No insertion, flushing, cleaning or medication in this lesson; contact a vet for pain, odor or discharge.

steps.title: Hand movement toward the ear
steps.teach: Offer the familiar chin target. While the dog chooses contact, move your other hand a little toward the outside of one healthy ear, stop and reward. End immediately if the chin lifts. Build only the comfortable hand approach, keeping fingers out of the canal. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Freely restarts and stays comfortable through the small hand approach in several turns.
steps.easier: Return to shoulder-level hand movement or the chin lesson. Do not investigate a painful ear through training.
steps.setup: With clean hands, sit beside your dog and prepare the familiar chin target and rewards. Work only around a healthy pain-free ear with room to withdraw; odor, discharge or pain needs a vet instead.

steps.title: A momentary outer-flap view
steps.teach: After a voluntary start, touch only the outer flap lightly as demonstrated by your veterinary team, then withdraw and reward. If appropriate, briefly lift just enough for an outside visual look without stretching. Let a lifted chin end contact. Practice the other side separately from the easiest level. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Voluntarily permits a momentary healthy outer-ear view on each side across two easy sessions.
steps.easier: Return to approach or one light touch. No cotton buds, instruments or treatment without veterinary instruction.
steps.setup: Use the veterinary team's demonstrated outer-flap approach, clean hands and the familiar chin start target. Keep rewards ready and all instruments away; no insertion, cleaning, flushing or medication is included. Work only with healthy, pain-free ears.

SIDELIE.title: Lie comfortably on one side
SIDELIE.goal: Choose a brief side-lying posture without being rolled or restrained.
SIDELIE.setup: A broad soft non-slip surface and comfortable movement. Skip for stiffness or breathing difficulty. This posture is not permission for procedures.

steps.title: Reward a natural hip roll
steps.teach: While your dog chooses a comfortable down, quietly reward a natural hip shift or brief roll toward one side. Feed where the head can remain neutral rather than twisting the neck. Invite a break after one reward. Capture the movement without pushing shoulders or pulling legs. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Offers a comfortable hip roll toward side-lying during several voluntary turns.
steps.easier: Reward a smaller hip shift or simply watch for a natural side rest. Do not manipulate the body.
steps.setup: Provide a broad soft non-slip resting area and sit beside it with quiet rewards. Begin during a voluntarily offered comfortable down, leaving head and limbs free; skip for stiffness or breathing difficulty.

steps.title: Brief full side rest
steps.teach: From the familiar hip roll, reward a little more voluntary shoulder lowering until the dog chooses to rest on one side. Mark the brief posture and reward low, then allow them to get up. Work in tiny pieces and keep all limbs free. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Chooses a brief full side rest and rises comfortably across two short sessions.
steps.easier: Return to a hip shift or stop. Do not continue if rising looks difficult.
steps.setup: Keep the familiar soft surface broad enough for a full side rest and easy rising. Sit at natural head level with rewards low and accessible, without placing hands against shoulders or legs.

steps.title: Name the offered position
steps.teach: Say “side” just before the familiar comfortable movement or small empty-hand invitation. Reward a moment in position and release. Gradually use less help without adding duration or touch. Teach either comfortable side separately; a single willing side is sufficient for this optional cue. Stop for tension, freezing or avoidance even if the start posture is held. Pause hands and tools immediately when the dog withdraws; never hold them in the start position.
steps.advance: Offers a brief side rest from the cue and small invitation in two sessions.
steps.easier: Keep capturing naturally offered rests. Any handling while side-lying needs a separate voluntary start and exit agreement.
steps.setup: Use the same comfortable resting surface and clear exit, with your invitation hand empty and rewards separate. Choose the dog's comfortable side; no handling procedure or increased hold is planned.

TAKE.title: Take a safe object
TAKE.goal: Pick up an offered suitable object voluntarily.
TAKE.setup: Light dog-safe object too large to swallow; no guarding or painful mouth.

steps.title: Shape gentle mouth contact
steps.teach: Hold the object still at an easy height. Initially mark a voluntary sniff and promptly reward. On later easy turns, mark a tiny open-mouth contact or gentle grip and promptly offer the reward, accepting release to eat or trade. Never put the object in the mouth or pull it out. Keep the criterion small enough for frequent success and put it aside only after willing release.
steps.advance: Voluntarily makes a gentle grip on most easy presentations without chewing or avoidance.
steps.easier: Try a different texture or lighter object; reward smaller mouth movements. Avoid food deprivation or forced holds.
steps.setup: Choose a light dog-safe object too large to swallow, without loose parts or a history of guarding. Sit beside your dog with rewards separate and the object at natural mouth height; skip for mouth pain.

steps.title: Add take before the offer
steps.teach: Say “take,” then present the object. Mark the gentle grip and promptly offer the reward, accepting voluntary release to eat or trade. Begin supporting less of the weight for a moment before marking. Finish before chewing begins. Do not pull the object from the mouth. This stage is pickup, not carrying across the room.
steps.advance: Takes the object on one cue on 4 of 5 presentations across two sessions, without a visible food lure.
steps.easier: Offer at a more comfortable height and shorten the grip; practice the release separately.
steps.setup: Use the familiar safe object at its successful height, with rewards out of sight and an easy trade ready. Leave open floor for any dropped object rather than arranging a carry route yet.

PULL.title: Tug a rope handle
PULL.goal: Gently pull one designated handle and release.
PULL.setup: Large intact rope handle, supervised; no mouth pain or guarding. Remove ropes after practice.

steps.title: Take the rope handle
steps.teach: Offer a large intact rope handle at comfortable mouth height. Mark a gentle voluntary grip and promptly offer the reward, allowing the dog to release to eat. On separate easy turns rehearse the known drop and reward it. No chewing, jumping or hard tug is needed. Use a handle that cannot catch feet or neck.
steps.advance: Willingly takes and releases this handle without chewing or tension.
steps.easier: Try a softer suitable handle and shorter grips. If teeth or neck appear uncomfortable, skip pulling.
steps.setup: Choose a large intact rope handle without loops that could catch feet or neck. Sit at comfortable mouth height with rewards and an easy drop trade ready; supervise and remove the rope afterward.

steps.title: Reward tiny backward tension
steps.teach: Hold the handle very lightly. As the dog grips, allow a tiny backward weight shift to create almost no resistance. Mark that small pull and promptly offer the reward, accepting release to eat. Rehearse the known drop separately if helpful. Do not yank against the dog or require a forceful neck movement.
steps.advance: Makes a small gentle pull and releases on 4 of 5 easy attempts.
steps.easier: Reward a smaller weight shift and remove all resistance.
steps.setup: Use the same safe rope handle on non-slip footing, with room for one tiny backward weight shift. Hold it lightly and prepare a release reward; do not attach it to resistance yet. Skip for mouth or neck pain or item guarding.

steps.title: Transfer to a lightweight hinged prop
steps.teach: Attach the handle securely to a stable lightweight training door or board that moves very easily without swinging into the dog. Cue the familiar grip and gentle pull, then reward a tiny movement. Build only enough movement to understand cause and effect.
steps.advance: Opens the easy prop with one gentle pull and releases on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Start with the prop already partly open and reward less movement. Avoid unstable furniture and hard resistance.
steps.setup: Secure the handle to a lightweight stable training hinge or board that moves very easily. Check that its swing cannot strike the dog, clear pinch points, and prepare rewards; avoid unstable furniture. Skip for mouth or neck pain or item guarding.

KEEP.title: Maintain skills and review changes
KEEP.goal: Keep useful cues rewarding and adapt to changing comfort.
KEEP.setup: Select a few useful skills; do not retest everything in one session.

steps.title: Plan short enjoyable refreshers
steps.teach: Choose one familiar useful skill and one optional fun activity in an easy setting. Reward generously and finish after a few good repetitions. Alternate activities across days if desired. Record only the exact step and setting you observed meeting its criterion; a successful refresher is not evidence for unobserved stages or harder contexts. There is no need to retrain demonstrated components unnecessarily.
steps.advance: A manageable refresher routine is recorded and remains enjoyable; no mandatory daily quota.
steps.easier: Use a single easy success and rest. More repetitions are not automatically better.
steps.setup: Select one familiar useful skill and an optional enjoyable activity. Prepare only their usual safe equipment in an easy setting, with rewards ready and enough time for a brief relaxed session.

steps.title: Review one trigger in comparable conditions
steps.teach: Use the session log to compare the same trigger and similar settings over time. Look at posture, comfort, and recovery, not just whether a cue was obeyed. If behavior worsens, reduce challenge, review health and environment, and seek help when needed.
steps.advance: A specific next adjustment is written from comparable observations; unanswered concerns have an appropriate follow-up.
steps.easier: Collect clearer observations at an easier level; leave unknown recovery values blank rather than entering zero.
steps.setup: Have your session log and comparable earlier observations open. Identify the same trigger and setting before reviewing; no new exposure or obedience test is needed, and unknown measurements can stay blank.

POSE.title: A comfortable photo pose
POSE.goal: Hold a chosen comfortable position for a quick photo.
POSE.setup: Use a known comfortable sit or stand; no costumes, forced handling, flash, or startling props.

steps.title: A very short still moment
steps.teach: Invite a comfortable familiar sit or stand. Mark a brief still moment and reward before your dog needs to move. Hold the phone down at first and reward comfort with it being present. Keep looking at your dog rather than repeatedly rearranging them.
steps.advance: Offers one or two comfortable still seconds with the ordinary phone present.
steps.easier: Use stand instead of sit, keep the phone farther away, or reward any comfortable pause.
steps.setup: Choose a familiar comfortable sit or stand area with non-slip footing. Hold the phone down, disable flash and startling sounds, and keep rewards ready; leave costumes and props out.

steps.title: Pair a quiet photo with a cue
steps.teach: Say “pose” before the familiar position signal. While the already easy brief pause is happening, take one silent no-flash photo, then mark and reward immediately and release. Do not extend the pause for a better picture. Keep the phone motion small; if the dog shifts or opts out, lower it and use an easier attempt next time.
steps.advance: Comfortably pauses for one quick no-flash photo in several easy attempts.
steps.easier: Return to phone presence without taking a picture. A photo is never worth extending discomfort.
steps.setup: Use the familiar pose area and check the camera is silent with flash off. Keep phone movements small, rewards accessible and an open release route; prepare just one brief photo opportunity.

CARDS.title: Respond to picture cue cards
CARDS.goal: Explore whether two simple visual symbols can cue two different familiar actions.
CARDS.setup: Two large distinct cards, a comfortable known sit or stand, and a known nose touch. Hold the card in one hand and keep the other empty target palm available in exactly the same position for both symbols; use a comfortable reset between trials.

steps.title: Pair one symbol with one known action
steps.teach: Choose a comfortable known sit or stand as the circle action. Hold the circle card in one hand while the other empty target palm stays still at an easy touch height; use this same palm position for both symbols. Show the card, briefly pause, then give the known position cue if needed. Reward the action, put the card away and reset to a comfortable free position. Never repeat cues after errors.
steps.advance: The first card begins to prompt its paired known action without repeated verbal requests.
steps.easier: Keep the usual verbal cue or stop the experiment. Never physically position the dog.
steps.setup: Two large distinct cards, a comfortable known sit or stand, and a known nose touch. Hold the card in one hand and keep the other empty target palm available in exactly the same position for both symbols; use a comfortable reset between trials.

steps.title: Pair the other symbol separately
steps.teach: In separate easy turns, show the striped card with the other empty target palm already available at exactly the same position used for the circle. Briefly pause, then give the familiar touch cue if needed. Reward the touch, remove the card and reset to a comfortable free position. Keep your posture unchanged; do not move the palm toward the dog to reveal the answer.
steps.advance: The second symbol begins to prompt its separate familiar action in a comfortable easy setup.
steps.easier: Use more distinct large symbols or return to ordinary cues. Avoid piling up unsuccessful guesses.
steps.setup: Two large distinct cards, a comfortable known sit or stand, and a known nose touch. Hold the card in one hand and keep the other empty target palm available in exactly the same position for both symbols; use a comfortable reset between trials.

steps.title: Alternate without hidden help
steps.teach: Present one card at a time in the same central position and a mixed order. Keep the empty target palm available at the same position for both cards, with matched posture and gaze. Begin each turn from a comfortable free reset. Reward the paired action; note responses before any old action cue. If gestures or old cues still guide choices, return to pairings or enjoy a simpler game. No literacy or intelligence claim follows.
steps.advance: Usually offers the paired action for each card across two brief mixed-order sessions. This is not evidence of literacy.
steps.easier: Re-pair each symbol separately. Any enjoyable learning is sufficient; no tests under pressure.
steps.setup: Two large distinct cards, a comfortable known sit or stand, and a known nose touch. Hold the card in one hand and keep the other empty target palm available in exactly the same position for both symbols; use a comfortable reset between trials.

CROSSPAW.title: Rest with crossed front paws
CROSSPAW.goal: Offer one light front-paw crossing while lying comfortably.
CROSSPAW.setup: A broad soft non-slip surface, comfortable down and a small willing paw offer. Skip if shoulders, elbows or wrists are uncomfortable; no held or forced crossing.

steps.title: A tiny reach in a down
steps.teach: With the dog in a comfortable down, offer the familiar low paw hand just a little toward the midline. Mark a tiny voluntary reach and let the paw return immediately. Reward without holding the foot or asking the dog to lean sideways. Keep early turns to one small reach.
steps.advance: Comfortably reaches the chosen paw slightly inward without shifting awkwardly or rising.
steps.easier: Offer the hand closer to the paw or reward a small lift. Never drag the leg across.
steps.setup: Provide a broad soft non-slip surface and wait for a comfortable voluntary down. Keep an empty receiving hand low near one front paw and rewards separate; skip for shoulder, elbow or wrist discomfort.

steps.title: Fade the receiving hand
steps.teach: Offer the same small inward invitation but lower your hand before contact so the dog can place the paw lightly across the other foreleg if comfortable. Mark the brief placement, promptly reward and allow the dog to uncross and move freely. Add “cross paws” before the invitation, fading the hand only across easy balanced turns.
steps.advance: Offers a brief voluntary light crossing from a cue and small signal across two sessions.
steps.easier: Reward the smaller reach again or skip the trick. A stretched, trapped or held leg is outside the goal.
steps.setup: Use the familiar soft surface and small inward invitation, with space for both forelegs to move freely. Keep rewards accessible and the receiving hand easy to lower; no limb is held or positioned. Skip for shoulder, elbow or wrist discomfort.

HOOP.title: Walk through a floor-level hoop
HOOP.goal: Choose to walk through a large opening without jumping.
HOOP.setup: A very wide smooth hoop held stationary with its bottom resting on the floor; no collars or tags that can snag.

steps.title: Explore the open shape
steps.teach: Keep the hoop still with its bottom on the floor and plenty of room to go around it. Reward a glance or approach. If comfortable, offer a known hand target or a small reward invitation through the center and reward one voluntary step through. Never move the hoop over the dog.
steps.advance: Walks through the large opening comfortably while it stays stationary on the floor.
steps.easier: Use a wider opening or stop at looking. Avoid hoops if tags, equipment, or body shape could snag.
steps.setup: Hold a very wide smooth hoop stationary with its bottom on the floor. Clear the route through and around it, check that equipment or tags cannot snag, and prepare the familiar target and rewards.

steps.title: Name the walking pass
steps.teach: Say “through” before the familiar invitation. Reward after the dog walks fully through. Gradually reduce your hand movement and hide any reward until after the pass while the hoop remains on the floor. Reset away from it so each pass is voluntary rather than a repetitive obstacle circuit.
steps.advance: Makes a relaxed walking pass on cue in 4 of 5 attempts across two short sessions.
steps.easier: Use the target again or end. This lesson does not add height, jumping, or narrow openings.
steps.setup: Use the familiar wide stationary hoop at floor level with clear approach and exit space. Keep any guiding hand empty and rewards ready beyond the opening; no jumping, narrowing or raised height is planned. Check tags and equipment cannot snag.

OPEN.title: Open a lightweight training prop
OPEN.goal: Open a purpose-built easy practice door with a gentle pull, during supervised play.
OPEN.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance.

steps.title: Make the practice door movement comfortable
steps.teach: Without a pulling task, let the dog notice the stable practice cabinet from a comfortable distance. Move its lightweight door a tiny amount with your hand, then promptly offer desired food. Stop the movement and allow retreat. Keep all paws, tail and face clear of travel and guarded hinges. No latch, seal or appliance is used.
steps.advance: Several small door movements remain comfortable across separate brief practices, with free retreat and ordinary recovery.
steps.easier: Use a smaller movement or greater distance, or skip the opening component and have a human present the retrieve prop.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance.

steps.title: Pull the easy door a tiny amount
steps.teach: Attach the familiar safe handle to the lightweight practice door, clear of feet and neck. A human controls the swing. Begin partly open, with almost no resistance. Cue the known gentle pull, mark a tiny opening and promptly reward, accepting release to eat. Stop for pawing, chewing or strain. Remove the handle after practice.
steps.advance: Gently moves the partly open practice door and releases without strain in most easy turns across separate short practices.
steps.easier: Have a human open it, use a smaller motion or return to the standalone gentle pull; do not increase resistance.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Prepare the familiar intact handle with no loop around the dog.

steps.title: Name the small supervised opening
steps.teach: Say “open” just before the familiar gentle pull on the practice door. Start from the easy gap, reward the small useful opening and accept release. Vary the starting gap only slightly on another practice; the door always moves freely without a catch. Keep the human controlling travel. Put the training prop away when finished; this does not authorize opening household cabinets.
steps.advance: Opens this freely moving practice door on the chosen cue from the practiced gap in most comfortable turns on separate practices.
steps.easier: Use the easier gap or a human-opened retrieve. Never add a seal, latch, heavy door or appliance.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Use the same familiar handle and starting gap.

CLOSE.title: Nudge a lightweight training door
CLOSE.goal: Gently nudge a human-controlled practice door during supervised play.
CLOSE.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance.

steps.title: Transfer a nose target to a large pad
steps.teach: Present the familiar broad target pad near a stationary lightweight practice door. Reward gentle nose contact while you hold it still. Attach the pad securely at a comfortable nose height, then reward the same touch without moving the door. Keep paws and tail clear; door motion is a separate next step. Use a purpose-built prop with guarded hinges, no latch and no food or electrical appliance.
steps.advance: Touches the pad gently on 4 of 5 presentations across two sessions.
steps.easier: Show the pad next to the hand again or reward a small nose approach.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Prepare the familiar broad secure target pad at comfortable nose height.

steps.title: Add a tiny moving-door push
steps.teach: Put the secure target at nose height on an easy lightweight door, with your hand controlling motion. Start almost closed. Reward a nose touch that moves it only an inch; protect paws and tail. Gradually ask for just enough push to close softly. Use only the purpose-built practice prop; no latch, seal, heavy door or appliance.
steps.advance: Can gently close the lightweight practice door on most attempts without pawing or slamming.
steps.easier: Reduce the gap and support the door more. Stop if motion or sound is worrying.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Place the secure broad nose target where the dog can touch without reaching into the gap.

steps.title: Name a gentle practice-door nudge
steps.teach: With the same lightweight guarded practice door almost closed, say “close” before the known gentle nose target. Mark a small useful nudge and promptly reward. Keep your hand controlling the door so it cannot slam or pinch. The target may stay. Human handling completes closure; never apply this exercise to a refrigerator or other appliance.
