steps.advance: Gently nudges the practice door on the chosen cue in most comfortable turns across separate practices, without pawing or slamming.
steps.easier: Keep the larger target, reduce movement or leave all closure to the human.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Keep the familiar broad target secure and the starting gap tiny.

SHELF.title: Retrieve from a low practice shelf
SHELF.goal: Pick up an empty safe carrier from a reachable practice shelf and deliver it gently.
SHELF.setup: An empty robust lightweight dog-safe carrier with a broad safe grip, and a stable low open practice shelf at natural mouth height. No contents, bottles, cans, small closures, food-storage cabinet or appliance; all feet remain on the floor.

steps.title: Practice an empty carrier near you
steps.teach: Present an empty robust lightweight carrier with a broad dog-safe grip and no loose parts. Use the familiar take, momentary hold and give, marking delivery and promptly rewarding. Inspect it between turns and stop for chewing or damage. Keep it empty; no bottles, cans, caps or food are needed. This is a gentle hand-delivery component, not an appliance task.
steps.advance: Takes and delivers the protected prop gently on most easy attempts; no chewing or damage.
steps.easier: Use an empty lighter carrier or ordinary toy. If the dog crushes, punctures, or guards it, skip this module.
steps.setup: Prepare an empty robust lightweight carrier with a broad safe grip and no detachable pieces. Inspect it for damage; sit or stand close on a clear non-slip floor with rewards ready.

steps.title: Pick up from an easy mock shelf
steps.teach: Place the same empty safe carrier on a stable low surface at a natural mouth height, directly next to you. Cue fetch, receive with give, and reward. Gradually add a step of carrying. The dog keeps all paws on the floor; no jumping, climbing, or stretching into a deep shelf.
steps.advance: Picks up from this reachable surface and delivers gently on 4 of 5 attempts in two sessions.
steps.easier: Move the carrier nearer the shelf edge or use a lower stable surface.
steps.setup: Set the familiar empty safe carrier on a stable low open practice shelf at natural mouth height. Clear a short non-slip delivery route; all paws stay on the floor, with no appliance or deep reach.

steps.title: Retrieve through the open practice doorway
steps.teach: Have a human hold the lightweight practice door safely open. Place the same empty safe carrier at the very front of a reachable low shelf, with no need to put the head or body inside the cabinet. Cue the known pickup and give, then mark delivery and reward. Add only a small delivery distance on later turns. Opening and closing stay separate.
steps.advance: Comfortably picks up the empty carrier from the open practice prop and delivers gently across separate short practices, with all paws on the floor.
steps.easier: Use an ordinary open shelf or present the carrier near you. Skip any arrangement requiring reaching into a confined gap.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Secure a reachable low shelf and place the familiar empty carrier at its front edge.

POUCH.title: Carry a little pouch
POUCH.goal: Carry a safe light message pouch a short distance.
POUCH.setup: A soft oversized empty pouch with a broad safe grip; no straps that can loop over the head and no contents to ingest.

steps.title: Take and return the empty pouch
steps.teach: Offer the familiar safe grip area and cue a known take. Allow a momentary gentle hold, then use the known give; mark delivery and promptly reward. If you mark an earlier grip, reward immediately and allow release instead of requiring another action first. Keep the pouch empty. The dog should not grip a zipper, buckle or narrow cord.
steps.advance: Takes, gently holds, and gives the empty pouch with no chewing or worry.
steps.easier: Use an ordinary safe retrieve toy. Remove straps or choose a different prop.
steps.setup: Inspect a soft oversized empty pouch with a broad safe grip. Remove head-catching straps and avoid gripping zips, buckles or cords; sit at a comfortable presentation height with rewards and a receiving palm ready.

steps.title: Carry toward a nearby hand
steps.teach: Offer the empty pouch, take one slow step back, and invite the familiar give into your hand. Reward after delivery. Build only a few steps, keeping the pouch off the ground and the route clear without asking for a prolonged hold.
steps.advance: Comfortably carries the empty pouch a few steps and gives on cue.
steps.easier: Return to a stationary give or one step. Stop if the load or grip changes natural movement.
steps.setup: Use the familiar empty pouch and clear a short straight non-slip carry route. Keep the safe grip at comfortable mouth height, a receiving hand close and rewards ready; no added load is needed.

steps.title: One light protected note
steps.teach: If the pouch is designed to stay closed and your dog is not a shredder, add a single protected paper note with no staples or clips. Repeat the familiar short carry. The human handles opening and closing; the dog only transports the safe prop.
steps.advance: Carries the very light closed pouch and gives it reliably without chewing or inspecting the contents.
steps.easier: Keep it empty or use a toy messenger game. Never add medication, valuables, or heavy contents.
steps.setup: Only use a pouch designed to stay closed with a dog that does not shred it. Secure one protected paper note without staples or clips inside, check the safe grip, and keep the familiar short route clear.

SCENTMATCH.title: Find one familiar person’s scent
SCENTMATCH.goal: Explore a learned choice between one familiar human-scent sample and a blank; not general matching to a new reference odor.
SCENTMATCH.setup: One willing familiar adult, large identical ventilated containers with secured lids, clean cotton samples and clean handling tools. No essential oils, chemicals or ingestible loose samples. One dog at a time; this is a game, not detection certification.

steps.title: A pleasant scent-container pairing
steps.teach: Let a familiar adult handle a clean cotton sample, then secure it inside a large vented container the dog cannot open or mouth. Present the container still and reward a voluntary sniff nearby from your hand. Put it away between turns. Keep rewards outside so scent and food are not stored together.
steps.advance: Comfortably investigates the safe container during several brief rewarding presentations.
steps.easier: Use a larger secured container or reward looking first. Stop for biting or frustrated pawing.
steps.setup: Have a willing familiar adult handle clean cotton, then secure it inside a large ventilated container the dog cannot open or mouth. Keep rewards outside the container, with no oils, chemicals or loose samples accessible.

steps.title: Introduce a clean comparison
steps.teach: Prepare matched cotton samples and identical safe vented containers using clean tools. One sample is handled by the chosen familiar adult; the comparison has no intentional sample from that person. Match other handling and keep food away from both. Reward a voluntary sniff at the familiar-person sample. Vary sides with neutral body language; after errors, make the next presentation easier without correction. A blank still has background odors.
steps.advance: Comfortably chooses to investigate the familiar sample more often than a fixed side across easy mixed positions.
steps.easier: Return to one container, use fresher samples and check accidental food odors or handling differences.
steps.setup: Using clean tools, prepare two identical secured vented containers: one familiar-adult cotton sample and one untouched sample. Place them equally near, keep food separate and other dogs away, and avoid differing handling odors.

steps.title: Try fresh samples of the same familiar odor
steps.teach: Prepare fresh matched samples and containers using the same careful handling. A helper changes their positions while you avoid pointing or watching the target. Give the familiar trained cue and reward a voluntary choice of the same familiar person’s sample. Keep comparison handling and containers balanced and record first choices. This explores one learned odor versus a blank; it does not establish matching a new person to a reference sample.
steps.advance: Most choices follow the familiar adult’s fresh sample across two short mixed-position sets with neutral human cues.
steps.easier: Keep the one-sample sniff game. A small household exercise does not establish operational detection or general matching ability.
steps.setup: Prepare fresh matched cotton samples and identical secured vented containers, with clean tools and a helper. Use the same familiar adult as before, keep food away from samples, balance other handling and plan mixed positions.

TRACKPERSON.title: Follow a short human trail
TRACKPERSON.goal: Enjoy following a short fresh familiar-person route; this recreational game does not certify tracking or identification.
TRACKPERSON.setup: Two familiar adults, a safe open low-distraction area, a secured familiar-human cotton scent sample and comfortable equipment if needed. Food stays at the finish, not along the route. No roads, forced separation or real missing-person searches.

steps.title: A very short visible route
steps.teach: Have a familiar adult walk a straight route of a few metres across clear safe ground and wait in view. Invite the dog to investigate from the start and follow at their pace, rewarding at the adult. Record the route beforehand. This visible introduction builds enjoyment rather than establishing tracking ability.
steps.advance: Comfortably investigates along the tiny route and enjoys the reward at the familiar adult.
steps.easier: Keep the adult closer or walk together. Skip if even brief distance causes distress.
steps.setup: Choose clear safe ground away from roads and two familiar adults, with one waiting visibly a few metres away. Use comfortable equipment if needed, note the short straight route and keep food only at the finish.

steps.title: Start a fresh unobserved trail
steps.teach: Let the dog remain comfortably with you while the familiar adult walks a fresh short straight route out of view and waits just behind a broad safe screen. Start where the route begins, say “track” and follow relaxed investigation without steering. Reveal the endpoint before frustration. A comfortably familiar secured scent sample may be offered, but it does not establish reference matching or prove which cues guide the dog.
steps.advance: Investigates from the start and follows the short freshly laid route toward the hidden endpoint on several easy turns.
steps.easier: Restore a visible finish or shorten the route. Do not hold the dog back, drag along the route or keep a helper hidden while distress develops.
steps.setup: Keep the dog comfortably with you while the familiar helper lays a fresh short straight route to a safe broad screen. Prepare their cotton sample in a secured container at the start, clean equipment and an easily revealed endpoint. Keep the route away from roads.

steps.title: One fresh broad bend
steps.teach: Have the adult lay a fresh route of roughly five to ten metres with one broad bend while the dog cannot see the departure. Mark the route for the humans and keep the finish easy. Invite from the scent sample at the start, follow without directional help and reward at the adult. If the dog takes a direct shortcut, simplify rather than counting it as route-following. A scent sample can be omitted. Ground disturbance, airborne odor and other cues may contribute; this is not a test of person-specific tracking.
steps.advance: Across two short sessions, willingly follows the approximate fresh route including its bend to the hidden adult. This is a small practiced trail, not evidence of operational tracking ability.
steps.easier: Return to a shorter straight trail or a visible finish. Keep trails fresh and easy; no aged tracks, unknown people or prolonged searches.
steps.setup: Arrange a fresh five-to-ten-metre route with one broad bend on safe ground while the dog comfortably stays with you. Mark it for the humans, prepare the helper's secured scent sample and an easy finish with rewards, away from roads.

SCENTINDICATE.title: Show a find with a quiet nose hover
SCENTINDICATE.goal: Offer a brief nose hover beside a safe secured scent container instead of grabbing it. This recreational routine does not establish identification of an unknown odor or operational detection ability.
SCENTINDICATE.setup: A large secured vented container with a familiar human cotton scent sample inside. No oils or loose samples. Comfortable natural head height, no prolonged breath holding or sustained nose pressure.

steps.title: Reward a brief investigation
steps.teach: Present the familiar secured scent container at an easy natural height. Mark the first brief nose investigation before licking, pawing or grabbing starts, reward away and reset. Keep turns short and reward early. The container stays fixed rather than being pushed into the dog’s face.
steps.advance: Offers gentle brief investigation without mouthing or pawing in several easy turns.
steps.easier: Reward a glance or approach from farther away. Remove the prop if chewing or frustration starts.
steps.setup: Secure the familiar human-cotton scent sample in a large ventilated container at natural head height. Fix it against movement, keep rewards separate and leave room to reset away; no oils or loose samples are accessible.

steps.title: A still moment beside the scent
steps.teach: After easy investigation, delay the marker by only a fraction of a second while the nose remains near the container. Reward before the dog presses or paws. Name the short hover “show me,” then reset away. Build to about one second at most, mixing immediate rewards in.
steps.advance: Offers a brief relaxed nose hover beside the container on invitation across two sessions.
steps.easier: Mark sooner and reward one soft investigation. Do not demand contact, a rigid freeze or a long hold.
steps.setup: Use the same fixed scent container at comfortable natural head height, with rewards accessible away from it. Keep the dog's head free and turns brief; no nose pressure or prolonged hold is planned.

ARTICLE.title: Find a familiar scented article
ARTICLE.goal: Locate a safe familiar-human-scented container in a small accessible area without retrieving it. This recreational routine does not establish identification of an unknown odor or operational detection ability.
ARTICLE.setup: A large secured vented container holding clean cotton handled by one familiar adult, safe open hiding places and no accessible samples, oils or food inside. This is recreational searching.

steps.title: An obvious scent destination
steps.teach: Present the familiar scent container on a clear floor while the dog watches. Say “find the article,” allow approach and investigation, and reward beside it from your hand. Leave the container where it is rather than inviting pickup. Move the obvious position slightly between short turns.
steps.advance: Comfortably locates and investigates the visible container without trying to retrieve it.
steps.easier: Keep it near your feet or reward a glance first. Secure the container or stop if it is mouthed.
steps.setup: Place the familiar secured human-scent container visibly on a clear floor, with food rewards separate in your hand. Keep samples, oils and container contents inaccessible, and leave space to investigate without pickup.

steps.title: A small concealed search
steps.teach: Let the dog watch the familiar container placed partly behind a broad safe object. Invite the search, remain neutral and reward discovery beside the container. Later make one easy placement while the dog looks away nearby. Keep the area tiny and reveal the container before frustration develops.
steps.advance: Willingly finds the container at several easy partly hidden placements across two sessions.
steps.easier: Show more of the container or use a visible placement. No inaccessible cavities, climbing or prolonged searching.
steps.setup: Prepare a tiny search area and a broad stable object partly screening the familiar secured container. Leave the access route open and rewards outside it, with the dog comfortably nearby and no climbing or cavities.

DRINK.title: Retrieve from a training prop
DRINK.goal: Combine a gentle practice-door opening, empty-carrier retrieval and delivery in a supervised enrichment game.
DRINK.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Use the familiar empty safe carrier on its reachable front shelf.

steps.title: Rehearse the easy delivery ending
steps.teach: With the human holding the practice door open, rehearse the easy empty-carrier pickup and give while you stand close. Mark delivery and reward generously. On other easy turns present the carrier near you for a familiar take and give. Keep the ending fluent and enjoyable before adding earlier links.
steps.advance: Easy deliveries from the open practice prop remain comfortable and gentle across separate short practices.
steps.easier: Present the carrier near you or use a simple open-shelf retrieve; do not add opening yet.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Use the familiar empty safe carrier on its reachable front shelf.

steps.title: Add the learned prop opening
steps.teach: Begin beside the familiar practice cabinet with its freely moving door at the easy starting gap. Cue the known opening and reward it; accept release to eat. Then cue the familiar shelf pickup and give and reward delivery. As the short sequence becomes easy, gradually use fewer intermediate rewards while keeping final delivery worthwhile. A terminal marker always receives its promised reward.
steps.advance: Opening, empty-carrier pickup and delivery work comfortably with familiar component cues in most easy turns across separate practices.
steps.easier: Split the components again or let a human open the prop. Restore intermediate rewards when a link becomes hesitant.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Use the familiar empty safe carrier on its reachable front shelf. Place rewards ready for both the opening and the delivery.

steps.title: Choose a human or dog closing finish
steps.teach: Human closure is a complete ending. If choosing an extra dog nudge, first complete CLOSE-4. Rehearse that ending separately with a human-opened empty practice prop: invite a short return to its target, reward the gentle nudge and finish. Then add it after an easy retrieve, rewarding delivery before the optional return. Keep your hand controlling door travel.
steps.advance: The chosen ending is comfortable across separate short practices. Dog closure is optional and used only after its own learned component.
steps.easier: Have the human close the prop or leave it safely open until the dog has moved away.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Use the familiar empty safe carrier on its reachable front shelf. Decide the ending in advance; dog nudging uses the familiar secure target.

steps.title: Introduce one request for the small routine
steps.teach: Say the final request just before the familiar easy prop sequence and supply the known component cues as needed. Across successful short practices, pause briefly before one extra cue so the next learned action can occur. Fade only that prompt; keep all movements and distance easy. Reward delivery and any separately chosen closing action. Finish and remove the prop and handle yourself.
steps.advance: Enjoys the selected short prop routine after the chosen request with little extra prompting across separate practices; finishes comfortably.
steps.easier: Restore a component cue or return to a shorter human-opened retrieve. No unattended practice, appliance transfer or useful-service certification is implied.
steps.setup: A stable lightweight purpose-built practice cabinet with rounded edges, guarded hinge gaps and no latch or seal. A human controls its easy door travel. Use a non-slip floor and remove the prop and handle after supervised practice. Never use an electrical or food-storage appliance. Use the familiar empty safe carrier on its reachable front shelf.

project.parallel: Practice prop-door comfort, gentle pulling, empty-carrier retrieval and optional nudging separately. Combine only the exact learned components. Human opening or closing is always a valid simpler game. This project never uses a refrigerator or other appliance.

SCENTREPORT.title: Find, show and report a scent
SCENTREPORT.goal: Find the familiar scent container, indicate it briefly, then return to touch the handler’s hand. This recreational routine does not establish identification of an unknown odor or operational detection ability.
SCENTREPORT.setup: One secured familiar human-scent container, easy accessible placements and an uncluttered room. No oils, operational searches or prolonged indication.

steps.title: Join the find and indication
steps.teach: Place the familiar container in a fully visible nearby spot. Invite the known article search, then the short nose-hover indication. Reward beside the find before any frustration or grabbing. Rehearse this ending separately from hidden placements and keep the container fixed throughout.
steps.advance: Finds and briefly indicates the visible container with comfortable component cues.
steps.easier: Reward discovery without the hover or rehearse the indication alone. Keep the task easy enough to avoid repeated prompting.
steps.setup: Fix the familiar secured human-scent container in a fully visible nearby floor-level spot. Keep food outside it and accessible beside the find, with room for a soft nose hover and no loose samples or oils.

steps.title: Add a close return report
steps.teach: After an easy find and hover, offer your familiar hand target a step away. Reward the touch at your hand and release. Alternate rewards at the find with rewards after the return so indicating remains worthwhile. Keep yourself close enough that leaving the find is an easy choice.
steps.advance: Comfortably changes from the short indication to a one-step hand-touch report.
steps.easier: Bring your hand closer or reward at both locations. Do not withhold rewards to force a longer chain.
steps.setup: Use the same visible fixed container and stand only a clear step away. Keep your target hand empty and rewards accessible both beside the find and at your hand, with an unobstructed return route.

steps.title: A tiny hidden search and report
steps.teach: Place the familiar secured container partly behind a broad safe object in the small known area. Say “report,” then support the known search, brief show and return touch with component cues. Reward generously, then finish. Gradually fade one extra prompt at a time without making the hiding harder.
steps.advance: Finds the easy container, briefly shows it and returns to touch with ordinary support across two sessions.
steps.easier: Reveal the container or return to the visible ending. This recreational chain does not certify an independent working alert.
steps.setup: Partly screen the familiar secured container behind a broad stable object in the tiny known search area. Keep all access open, stand nearby with an empty target hand, and have rewards and component cues ready.

sources.title: Managing Mask Phobia in Dogs
sources.author: Tufts Cummings School; Stephanie Borns-Weil
sources.finding: Pairs distant unfamiliar appearances with rewards and reduces difficulty if distress appears.
sources.limits: Specific example, not a controlled comparison. Greeting at close distance need not be the owner's goal.
sources.use: Stranger appearance and movement stages; separate generalization.

sources.title: Fears and Phobias in Dogs: Animals and People
sources.author: VCA veterinary authors
sources.finding: Use medical assessment, controlled gradients, and retreat rather than forced proximity or feeding.
sources.limits: Individual diagnosis and bite-risk planning require direct assessment.
sources.use: Strangers and other dogs; handler supplies rewards without luring toward the trigger.

sources.title: How to introduce a marker to your dog training
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: A consistent signal followed by a reward can identify the action being reinforced.
sources.limits: Does not demonstrate clickers are superior to food-only teaching.
sources.use: Simple marker setup; use a soft word for sound-sensitive dogs.

sources.title: Getting Your Dog's Focus And Attention
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Builds a positive response to the dog's name and handler attention.
sources.limits: Responding around triggers is a separate contextual challenge.
sources.use: A short two-stage name guide; avoid unnecessary subdivisions.

sources.title: Train your dog to touch a target
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Teaches voluntary nose or paw targeting using gradual reinforcement.
sources.limits: Practical guide rather than a clinical anxiety-treatment trial.
sources.use: Hand target and object target foundations.

sources.title: How to train your dog to leave it
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Distinguishes trading an item already held from leaving an item before taking it.
sources.limits: Generic exercises do not treat established resource guarding safely on their own.
sources.use: Separate leave and drop skills; reward away from the practice object.

sources.title: Dealing with resource guarding
sources.author: Battersea canine behavior team
sources.finding: Avoid confrontation and punishment; give space and use safe management/exchanges. Seek help for serious concerns.
sources.limits: Do not use approach-to-bowl advice as a generic home treatment for a dog already guarding.
sources.use: Guarding boundary for food, toys, retrieval, and equipment work.

sources.title: Teach your dog to walk nicely on a lead
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Reward proximity and build movement gradually in easy settings.
sources.limits: Standing still during pulling is not appropriate if a fearful dog needs to escape a trigger.
sources.use: Loose-leash acquisition; use escape instead during anxiety incidents.

sources.title: How to train your dog to come back when called
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Make returning rewarding; use secure environments or a long line on a harness during practice.
sources.limits: No recall is a replacement for physical management around roads, animals, or known triggers.
sources.use: Recall foundation and later separate practice elsewhere.

sources.title: Teaching Your Dog To Stay
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Build brief duration and handler movement with rewards delivered in position.
sources.limits: A stay is an operant posture task and does not by itself change fear.
sources.use: Separate duration and distance from the initial sit/down skill.

sources.title: How to teach your dog to sit
sources.author: Battersea canine behavior team
sources.finding: Uses food guidance, an empty hand signal, and then a verbal cue.
sources.limits: Avoid physically positioning the dog; discomfort may require a different posture and vet review.
sources.use: Compact sit acquisition with lure fading.

sources.title: How to train your dog to wear a harness
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Choose comfortable equipment and introduce it gradually with rewards.
sources.limits: A harness is management, not a cure for pulling or fear; individual fit matters.
sources.use: Equipment comfort; strong-dog handling based on fit and control.

sources.title: How to Stop Your Dog Jumping Up at People
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Reward an alternative greeting behavior for happy greeters; fear-related jumping needs emotional support first.
sources.limits: Do not force a greeting or wait out a frightened dog near a person.
sources.use: Four-paws greeting only with already-comfortable familiar people.

sources.title: How to Teach Your Dog to Fetch
sources.author: Sassafras Patterdale, CPDT-KA, CTDI; AKC
sources.finding: Breaks retrieval into object interest, gentle holding, pickup, and gradual movement/distance.
sources.limits: Practical guidance, not proof that a retrieval task treats anxiety. Page contains affiliate links, which are not recommendations here.
sources.use: Original take/hold/carry/give progression and task chains.

sources.title: Teach your dog to tidy up their toys
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Combines picking up, holding, dropping, and a destination target.
sources.limits: Multi-part task requires component fluency; timeline varies.
sources.use: Toy cleanup chain with individual teachable steps.

sources.title: How to Teach Your Pet to Target
sources.author: Laurie Luck, KPA CTP; Karen Pryor Clicker Training
sources.finding: Target placement can transfer learned touches into useful movements and household tasks.
sources.limits: Commercial training publisher; procedural guidance, not an anxiety trial.
sources.use: Door-closing target and original household task adaptations.

sources.title: Chin Rests: Practical Uses and Teaching Your Dog
sources.author: Stephanie Gibeault, MSc, CPDT; AKC
sources.finding: A chin target can provide a voluntary stationary position for gentle handling practice.
sources.limits: Do not infer calm merely from the posture or continue after withdrawal. Workbook explicitly stops handling when the chin lifts.
sources.use: Chin rest acquisition and a separate handling program.

sources.title: Separation Anxiety
sources.author: ASPCA behavior guidance
sources.finding: Graduated absences should stay shorter than the onset of distress; severe cases need individual support.
sources.limits: A food toy or crate is not a sufficient treatment for panic. A learned stay is not evidence of comfort alone.
sources.use: Optional very-short absence foundations; camera monitoring, no cry-it-out.

sources.title: People Foods to Avoid Feeding Your Pets
sources.author: ASPCA Poison Control
sources.finding: Alcohol is toxic to pets, as are several common foods and ingredients.
sources.limits: Toxicity depends on substance and exposure; a training plan must prevent access rather than estimate a safe ingestion amount.
sources.use: Use a sealed water-bottle prop in a carry sleeve for the fridge chain; never offer alcohol.

sources.title: Sounds Scary booklet
sources.author: Dogs Trust
sources.finding: Uses adjustable recordings and stops/reduces the sound if fear appears.
sources.limits: Contains older advice discouraging reassurance; that advice is rejected in favor of current guidance. Recording success does not establish readiness for real storms.
sources.use: Historical cross-check only. Do not adopt its instruction to withhold comfort; use R06, P27 and P28 for current noise guidance.

sources.title: Helping your dog cope with fireworks
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Supports comfortable hiding, trusted company, reduced exposure, and calm comfort when sought.
sources.limits: Educational guidance; any sound-masking product claims are not treated here as clinical proof.
sources.use: Real-event plan; replaces older advice to withhold reassurance.

sources.title: Fear of fireworks and thunderstorms
sources.author: Aly Cohen and Kate Anderson; Cornell veterinary medicine
sources.finding: Encourages a comfortable safe space and veterinary planning before severe predictable noise events.
sources.limits: A crate is useful only if already comfortable; adjuncts need individual veterinary assessment.
sources.use: Real-event support and professional escalation.

sources.title: Should You Use a Secondary Reinforcer (Clicker) in Counter Conditioning?
sources.author: AVSAB educational article
sources.finding: Separates marking an operant behavior from pairing a feared event directly with food.
sources.limits: Some cited experimental evidence is from humans, not a direct canine clinical comparison.
sources.use: Do not make fear-reward pairings contingent on an obedience response or a marker.

sources.title: Case Study: Luna — Reactivity to Other Dogs Part 1
sources.author: IAABC Foundation Journal case author
sources.finding: Describes adapted handling, a rewarded U-turn, barriers, and voluntary disengagement while monitoring medical issues.
sources.limits: Single case narrative, not randomized evidence for a named game. Does not validate a universal distance or treatment success rate.
sources.use: Practical context for original walk-escape and disengagement guides.

sources.title: How to train your dog to travel in the car
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: Build comfortable participation around a stationary car, equipment, sound, and travel gradually.
sources.limits: Training cannot rule out nausea or pain. No jurisdiction-specific legal advice is adopted.
sources.use: Optional car-comfort guide, separate from roadside trigger work.

sources.title: Brain games for dogs
sources.author: Battersea canine behavior team
sources.finding: Offers practical food-search and puzzle activities using suitable portions of the daily diet.
sources.limits: Enrichment guidance is not evidence that games alone treat clinical anxiety.
sources.use: Food searches and low-pressure enrichment; avoid overfeeding.

sources.title: Position Statement on Humane Dog Training
sources.author: American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior
sources.finding: Recommends reward-based teaching and humane behavior treatment; identifies welfare risks from aversive methods.
sources.limits: Position statement synthesizing heterogeneous studies; not a randomized anxiety-treatment trial.
sources.use: Overall training approach; professional referral; avoid punishment and flooding.

sources.title: Changing behaviors: AAHA behavior management guidelines
sources.author: AAHA behavior guidelines task force
sources.finding: Management, behavior modification, and sometimes medication form an integrated plan. Exposure should be gradual; flooding can worsen distress.
sources.limits: Older clinical guidance; some terminology/examples on the page are imprecise. Use the clinical principles rather than reproduce those examples.
sources.use: Exposure design, prevention of overwhelming practice, management.

sources.title: Does training method matter? Evidence for the negative impact of aversive-based methods on companion dog welfare
sources.author: Vieira de Castro et al.
sources.finding: Dogs in aversive-focused training schools showed more stress-related behavior and other adverse welfare measures than reward-focused groups.
sources.limits: School choice was not randomized; welfare study, not a test of comparative training efficacy. Confounding remains possible.
sources.use: Welfare rationale for reward-based training.

sources.title: Efficacy of Dog Training With and Without Remote Electronic Collars vs. a Focus on Positive Reinforcement
sources.author: China, Mills and Cooper
sources.finding: Reward-focused training had favorable recall/sit response measures and did not require an electronic collar.
sources.limits: Trainer approaches and seasons differed; positive-reinforcement group not randomized with the other two groups. Recall evidence does not establish a cure for anxiety or aggression.
sources.use: Foundation training rationale; avoid claims that pain is necessary for a strong dog.

sources.title: Counterconditioning-based interventions for companion dog behavioural modification: A systematic review
sources.author: Shnookal, Tepper, Howell and Bennett
sources.finding: Most included reports had positive outcomes, but procedures varied between classical and operant approaches.
sources.limits: Small samples, heterogeneous methods, and expert involvement limit precise effectiveness estimates and generalization. Not a meta-analysis proving every named exercise.
sources.use: Distinguish changing feelings from rewarding an alternative behavior.

sources.title: Therapy and Prevention of Noise Fears in Dogs—A Review of the Current Evidence for Practitioners
sources.author: Stefanie Riemer
sources.finding: Reviews environmental management, sound training, reward pairing, relaxation, and veterinary medication. Recordings cannot reproduce every feature of real noise events.
sources.limits: Training results often come from caregiver surveys; medication trials have stronger controls. Product evidence varies.
sources.use: Noise plans, realistic expectations, veterinary discussion, and measurement.

sources.title: Effectiveness of treatments for firework fears in dogs
sources.author: Stefanie Riemer
sources.finding: Caregiver reports favored counterconditioning, relaxation, and some veterinary medications over many alternative products.
sources.limits: Self-selection, recall, and caregiver expectations; reported percentages are not randomized treatment effects.
sources.use: Context for noise plans; do not promise survey success rates.

sources.title: Ancestry-inclusive dog genomics challenges popular breed stereotypes
sources.author: Morrill et al.
sources.finding: Behavior varies substantially within breeds. Breed ancestry provides limited prediction of an individual dog's behavior, despite genetic and breed-associated tendencies.
sources.limits: Survey-based factors; not a dog-bite risk assessment or a trial of anxiety treatments.
sources.use: Tailor to the individual dog’s observed needs; do not infer a diagnosis from breed or appearance.

sources.title: Prevalence, comorbidity, and breed differences in canine anxiety in 13,700 Finnish pet dogs
sources.author: Salonen et al.
sources.finding: Anxiety-like traits can co-occur and differ between sampled breeds.
sources.limits: Convenience sample and owner reports; not an intervention trial or an individual prognosis.
sources.use: Track several triggers and avoid assuming all reactivity has one cause.

sources.title: Noise Sensitivities in Dogs: An Exploration of Signs in Dogs with and without Musculoskeletal Pain Using Qualitative Content Analysis
sources.author: Lopes Fagundes et al.
sources.finding: Noise-sensitive dogs with musculoskeletal pain showed patterns suggesting that pain assessment can matter, including later onset and wider generalization.
sources.limits: Small clinical sample; does not mean all fearful dogs have pain or that pain treatment alone resolves anxiety.
sources.use: Medical review for sudden change, touch sensitivity, or late-onset sound fear.

sources.title: The click is not the trick: the efficacy of clickers and other reinforcement methods in training naive dogs to perform new tasks
sources.author: Gilchrist, Gunter, Anderson and Wynne
sources.finding: Food alone, verbal markers plus food, and clicker plus food could teach behaviors; no consistent overall superiority of a clicker emerged.
sources.limits: Specific laboratory tasks and short training periods; markers may still be convenient for timing.
sources.use: Make a quiet verbal marker optional; do not require buying a clicker.

sources.title: Let me sniff! Nosework induces positive judgment bias in pet dogs
sources.author: Duranton and Horowitz
sources.finding: After a nosework program, dogs approached an ambiguous test location faster than before; control heelwork dogs did not show that pattern.
sources.limits: Cognitive-bias proxy and small sample; not evidence that sniffing cures reactivity or replaces treatment.
sources.use: Optional food-search enrichment and choice.

sources.title: The effect of frequency and duration of training sessions on acquisition and long-term memory in dogs
sources.author: Demant, Ladewig, Balsby and Dabelsteen
sources.finding: Session spacing and length affected acquisition for the studied task; more consecutive sessions were not automatically better.
sources.limits: One task, one laboratory population; better acquisition per session does not necessarily mean fewer calendar days. No universal ideal schedule established.
sources.use: Short sessions with rest; numerical session lengths in the guide are practical starting points.

sources.title: Behavioral rehabilitation of extremely fearful dogs: Report on the efficacy of a treatment protocol
sources.author: Collins et al., ASPCA
sources.finding: A structured specialist program helped many selected, severely fearful shelter dogs reach adoption criteria.
sources.limits: Intensive staffing, selected intake, multimodal care, and exclusion of several other behavior problems. Its graduation rate is not a home-training success prediction for dog-directed aggression.
sources.use: Hope with realistic scope; explain why professional individualized care can matter.

sources.title: Dexmedetomidine oromucosal gel for noise-associated acute anxiety and fear in dogs
sources.author: Korpivaara et al.
sources.type: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled field trial; 182 dogs
sources.finding: Owners reported better acute firework outcomes for active treatment than placebo.
sources.limits: Specific medication, noise context, and caregiver outcomes; industry affiliations. Does not establish effects on stranger fear or specify what this dog should take.
sources.use: Evidence for discussing veterinary help before unavoidable noise events; no dosing advice.

sources.title: Effectiveness of imepitoin for the control of anxiety and fear associated with noise phobia in dogs
sources.author: Engel et al.
sources.type: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial; 238 recruited dogs
sources.finding: Imepitoin reduced caregiver-rated noise fear compared with placebo in the studied fireworks setting.
sources.limits: Medication-specific adverse effects, including ataxia, need veterinary consideration. Manufacturer involvement; not a general training trial.
sources.use: Veterinary discussion of multimodal care; never a prescription or home dosing guide.

sources.title: Effect of a Standardized Four-Week Desensitization and Counter-Conditioning Training Program on Pre-Existing Veterinary Fear in Companion Dogs
sources.author: Stellato et al.
sources.finding: The short program produced limited measured improvements; adherence was a substantial difficulty.
sources.limits: Many owners did not comply; home practice and clinic handling varied. Does not show that a fixed four-week plan resolves veterinary fear.
sources.use: Realistic cooperative-care expectations and gradual individualized plans.

sources.title: Effect of cooperative care training on physiological parameters and compliance in dogs undergoing a veterinary examination: A pilot study
sources.author: Wess et al.
sources.finding: Physiological and compliance results were mixed; fewer trained dogs complied with temperature taking at the second visit.
sources.limits: Pilot sample and procedure-specific effects. Stillness and compliance should not be equated automatically with improved welfare.
sources.use: Teach voluntary handling as a useful skill while acknowledging limited direct efficacy evidence.

sources.title: Efficacy of a remote-controlled, positive-reinforcement, dog-training system for modifying problem behaviors exhibited when people arrive at the door
sources.author: Yin, Fernandez, Pagan, Richardson and Snyder
sources.type: Multi-step training experiments; lab 6 dogs, home 15 dogs
sources.finding: Owners could implement a detailed reward-based stationing protocol and reduce measured door-arrival problem behaviors.
sources.limits: Small samples and a specific protocol/device; not a large randomized treatment trial for severe visitor aggression. Device-related interests merit attention.
sources.use: Detailed component teaching for a door routine; no dispenser purchase required.

sources.title: The perception of pet owners on their dog's anxiety while supplemented with cannabidiol in a double-blinded randomized placebo-controlled cross-over clinical trial
sources.author: Corsato Alvarenga et al.
sources.finding: CBD did not reduce reported anxiety behaviors relative to placebo in this study; improvement over time occurred regardless of treatment.
sources.limits: Caregiver outcomes, study participation effects, tested formulation/population only; sponsor involvement in design and interpretation.
sources.use: Do not make CBD a required training purchase or promise anxiety relief.

sources.title: Does adolescent and adult training affect canine behavior problems?
sources.author: Dinwoodie, Keller and Dodman
sources.finding: Training history was associated with some reported behavior outcomes; training style was not significantly associated with outcomes in this analysis.
sources.limits: Observational, self-reported owner survey; confounding and selection bias; null associations for many outcomes do not show training has no effect.
sources.use: Recent-literature context; avoid claiming every study finds one training style universally superior.

sources.title: Use of classical conditioning and differential reinforcement via a treat dispenser in combination with behavior medication to treat separation related problems: A case study
sources.author: Gavin, Carlson and Sackman
sources.finding: Describes improvement during a combined medication, dispenser, and training plan.
sources.limits: One dog, several simultaneous interventions, no concurrent control; cannot establish superiority or a general time-to-success.
sources.use: Illustration of individualized multimodal work; not core efficacy evidence.

sources.title: Improving dog training methods: Efficacy and efficiency of reward and mixed training methods
sources.author: Vieira de Castro et al.
sources.type: Proposed study protocol; excluded from outcome evidence
sources.finding: Describes planned allocation and assessment of military/police dogs.
sources.limits: Future-tense methods; no completed results reported in this record.
sources.use: Saved as an evidence-screening example; not cited as proof of comparative efficacy.

sources.title: Comparison of the Efficacy and Welfare of Different Training Methods in Stopping Chasing Behavior in Dogs
sources.author: Johnson and Wynne
sources.finding: In this lure-chasing experiment, the shock-collar group stopped chasing during training whereas the tested non-aversive procedures did not; many collar-trained dogs resumed chasing in a novel arena.
sources.limits: Specific predatory task, protocol, small sample, and limited generalization; not a fear-treatment study. Few observed stress behaviors cannot establish absence of broader welfare risks.
sources.use: Important counterexample to any claim that reward-based methods outperform aversives in every experiment. Does not justify aversives for this anxiety guide.

sources.title: Effectiveness of marker training for detection dogs
sources.author: Lazarowski et al.
sources.finding: Markers aided some aspects of complex alert acquisition and precision in this detection task.
sources.limits: Purpose-bred working dogs, ball rewards, and precise operational responses; does not contradict the absence of a universal clicker advantage on simple pet tasks.
sources.use: Explain that a marker is useful but optional, and benefits are task-dependent.

sources.title: A preliminary examination of the contextual interference effect on trained trick retention in domestic dogs
sources.author: Messina et al.
sources.finding: Found no significant difference between blocked and randomized practice of three tricks in the tested conditions.
sources.limits: Small preliminary study; does not prove the schedules are equivalent or establish one optimal routine.
sources.use: Parallel practice is offered for convenience and component compatibility, not as a proven superior learning schedule.

sources.title: Impact of variations in training schedules on dogs’ acquisition and retention of an odor detection task
sources.author: Smith, Krichbaum, Rogers, Waggoner, Katz, and Lazarowski
sources.type: Experimental learning study; 48 purpose-bred detection dogs
sources.finding: A detection task showed different scheduling effects from the earlier obedience study; breaks and individual traits also mattered.
sources.limits: 48 purpose-bred detection dogs; working-dog odor task and one-week retention do not define pet-dog maintenance intervals. Publisher-indexed abstract/highlights only; full paper not reviewed.
sources.use: Support a flexible reminder rather than a universal required practice frequency.

sources.title: How to train your dog: top training tips
sources.author: RSPCA
sources.finding: Recommends reward-based teaching in brief, regular sessions, with patience for individual learning rates.
sources.limits: General reward-based guidance; does not define a measured forgetting interval or validate mandatory refresher frequency.
sources.use: Keep reminders gentle, easy to dismiss, and focused on comfortable, rewarded practice.

sources.title: Helping Dogs Cope with Fear and Big Emotions
sources.author: Dogs Trust
sources.finding: Lists subtle-to-overt signs of fear/stress and recommends considering medical issues and environment.
sources.limits: Signs are context-dependent; no single signal diagnoses an emotional state.
sources.use: Body language and readiness observations.

sources.title: Dog breeds directory
sources.author: American Kennel Club
sources.access: Public breed-name directory only; not a dog-training evidence source.
sources.finding: Breed names and varieties can be recorded as profile information.
sources.limits: A breed directory does not establish this individual dog’s behaviour. Mixes, unknown and unlisted names remain valid.
sources.use: Searchable profile labels only; directory temperament descriptions and ratings are not copied.

sources.title: AVSAB Position Statements (2025 board statement; 2021 Humane Dog Training statement remains current)
sources.author: AVSAB
sources.type: Veterinary professional consensus / position statement hub
sources.finding: AVSAB’s 2025 board statement confirms its 2021 Humane Dog Training position remains current and recommends reward-based methods for all dog training and behavior modification.
sources.limits: Professional consensus, not a randomized trial; hub page may change and should be paired with the linked position statement.
sources.use: Authoritative policy context.

sources.title: Dog bowling: Teach your dog to ten pin bowl
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.finding: A nose target can be developed into a floor-ball nudge and then movement toward lightweight pins.
sources.limits: Practical enrichment guidance, not evidence of an anxiety treatment. Ball size, noise, ingestion risk and supervision matter. Practical trick instruction, not evidence of general behavior change or anxiety treatment; keep movements comfortable and equipment/object size safe.
sources.use: Ball pushing, bowling and goal-game adaptations.

sources.title: How to teach your dog to read
sources.author: Dogs Trust behavior team
sources.type: Original professional trick guide; critically screened
sources.finding: The illustrated box game pairs spoken labels and gestures with going to designated boxes.
sources.limits: The procedure does not isolate visual discrimination of printed words from spoken cues, gestures, location, or box identity. It is an informal trick, not evidence of reading or literacy.
sources.use: Inspired a clearly labeled optional visual-cue experiment; no claim of literacy or language comprehension is made.

sources.title: How to Teach Your Dog to Weave Through Your Legs
sources.author: Stephanie Gibeault, MSc, CPDT / American Kennel Club
sources.finding: Separate comfortable passes around each side can be joined into a stationary figure eight, then optional walking passes.
sources.limits: A trick guide, not a clinical intervention or an exercise prescription. Tight turns and handler clearance need individual judgment. Practical trick instruction, not evidence of general behavior change or anxiety treatment; keep movements comfortable and equipment/object size safe.
sources.use: Comfortable middle position and slow stationary weave; cone alternatives for dogs that do not fit comfortably.

sources.title: Teach Your Dog to Bow
sources.author: AKC staff; demonstration by Nancy Field, CPDT-KA
sources.finding: Describes building a bow, fading the food prompt and adding a cue.
sources.limits: Not evidence that holding a bow treats anxiety or improves health. The app favors capturing a natural comfortable stretch and avoids physical positioning. Practical trick instruction, not evidence of general behavior change or anxiety treatment; keep movements comfortable and equipment/object size safe.
sources.use: Optional short bow with no forced stretching or prolonged hold.

sources.title: Successful Toothbrushing Training for Happy Dental Care
sources.author: VCA Animal Hospitals
sources.type: Veterinary professional care and training guide
sources.finding: Builds comfortable participation and small mouth-care components before introducing gentle brushing.
sources.limits: Dental pain or oral disease needs a veterinary examination. Toothbrush size, pet-safe paste and technique should be selected with the veterinary team.
sources.use: Voluntary toothbrushing preparation; no restraint, forced jaw opening, human toothpaste or dosing instructions.

sources.title: Investigating responses to object-labels in the domestic dog (Canis familiaris)
sources.author: Hanna Kőszegi, Claudia Fugazza, Lilla Magyari, Ivaylo B. Iotchev, Ádám Miklósi, Attila Andics
sources.finding: Examines responses to spoken object labels while attempting to distinguish name learning from other cues.
sources.limits: Twenty typical owner-nominated dogs with reported familiarity with a few labels; a group effect and only one individually reliable performer. Not literacy or evidence of a large reliable household vocabulary.
sources.use: Optional two-object choice experiment with side swaps, neutral body language and permission to stop.

sources.title: Rapid learning of object names in dogs
sources.author: Fugazza and colleagues / Scientific Reports
sources.finding: Two exceptional dogs learned novel object labels after four social exposures, with short retention; 20 typical family dogs did not demonstrate comparable learning.
sources.limits: Peer-reviewed word-learning study in a specialized sample/task; rapid label learning in selected dogs does not establish typical pet-dog expectations.
sources.use: Avoiding exaggerated claims about toy-name games, ‘reading’, fast mapping or dog intelligence.

sources.title: What is Trigger Stacking? How to Handle an Overly Stressed Dog
sources.author: American Kennel Club training contributors
sources.finding: Multiple close-together stressful events may leave a dog less able to cope with the next challenge.
sources.limits: Practical AKC explanation, not a precise physiological construct or experimentally validated recovery clock; avoid fixed “trigger stacking” thresholds.
sources.use: Reducing demands after a difficult day, using individual baseline observations rather than fixed decompression deadlines.

sources.title: How to train your dog: top training tips
sources.author: RSPCA
sources.finding: Recommends reward-based teaching in brief, regular sessions, with patience for individual learning rates.
sources.limits: General reward-based guidance; does not define a measured forgetting interval or validate mandatory refresher frequency.
sources.use: Keep reminders gentle, easy to dismiss, and focused on comfortable, rewarded practice.

sources.title: Crate training your dog
sources.author: PDSA
sources.finding: Voluntary introductions and gradual positive steps help make a suitable crate familiar.
sources.limits: A crate is not a treatment for separation distress. This app stops at tiny attended closures, not prolonged confinement.
sources.use: The separate attended crate-door lesson; exits and comfort remain available.

sources.title: Fear Free Handling
sources.author: SPCA New Zealand
sources.finding: Supports voluntary participation in routine care using cooperative approaches and low-stress handling.
sources.limits: A professional position statement, not a validated protocol for each care task. Pain and actual procedures need individual veterinary guidance.
sources.use: Start signals, stopping at withdrawal, and preparation rather than forced handling.

sources.title: Scent Work: Get Started
sources.author: American Kennel Club
sources.finding: Recreational scent work joins finding a scent with communicating the find to a handler.
sources.limits: The app uses secured familiar-human cotton samples without essential oils. Its games are original adaptations and do not establish competition readiness or operational detection.
sources.use: Separate scent search, indication and cooperative report components.

sources.title: Walking 1-2-3
sources.author: CattleDog Publishing veterinary behavior education team
sources.finding: Describes a predictable counting and reward pattern and credits Leslie McDevitt’s Control Unleashed pattern games.
sources.limits: Practical teaching guidance, not a clinical trial or a guarantee that the game will make trigger exposure safe.
sources.use: A short quiet count-and-walk adaptation with optional participation and no fear-exposure requirement.

sources.title: Tracking: Get Started
sources.author: American Kennel Club
sources.finding: Distinguishes following a human-laid scent route from simply finding a visible person or article.
sources.limits: A competition overview is not a validated training protocol. This app’s fresh tiny trails do not qualify a dog for sport or search-and-rescue work.
sources.use: Separating a recreational human-route-following exercise from visual hide-and-seek and food trails.

sources.title: Housetraining for Puppies and Dogs
sources.author: VCA Animal Hospitals
sources.finding: Explains supervision, regular opportunities, and positive reinforcement for elimination location.
sources.limits: Individual medical and developmental needs vary; veterinary check if behavior changes.
sources.use: Toileting curriculum and medical flags.

sources.title: Separation Anxiety in Dogs
sources.author: VCA Animal Hospitals
sources.finding: Recommends camera monitoring, below-distress departures, and stopping exercises if distress occurs.
sources.limits: Clinical guidance; cases that show distress need individualized veterinary support.
sources.use: Alone-time prerequisites, monitoring, progression.

sources.title: Training “stay” vs. “wait”
sources.author: Cornell University Riney Canine Health Center
sources.finding: Distinguishes a maintained stay from a brief wait and discusses cueing and generalization.
sources.limits: Educational guidance reprinted from a newsletter, not an experiment; concerns wait/stay, not evidence about default leave-it.
sources.use: Clarify how practical “default wait” language differs from the leave-it research question.

sources.title: Stimulus Control of Odorant Concentration: Pilot Study of Generalization and Discrimination of Odor Concentration in Canines
sources.author: DeChant, Bunker, and Hall
sources.type: Open-access pilot study; four detection dogs
sources.finding: Dogs showed limited spontaneous generalization across odor concentrations; discrimination training changed responding in a way that depended on training arrangement.
sources.limits: Four dogs, specialized olfactory apparatus, and working-dog detection task; no direct household behavior application.
sources.use: Illustrate that generalization is not automatic and that stimulus dimensions matter.

sources.title: Odour generalisation and detection dog training
sources.author: Caldicott et al.
sources.finding: Reviews how exemplar variation, discrimination, and stimulus control affect odor generalization in detection work.
sources.limits: Specialized working-dog review; household skill transfer is indirect.
sources.use: Support explicit generalization planning as a design principle, with limits stated.

sources.title: Training Does Not Uniformly Increase Canine Self-Control
sources.author: Silver, Singer, Welch, Perry, Jones, Cates, and Furlong
sources.finding: Agility, barn-hunt, and scent-work dogs did not show a uniform advantage on the tested cylinder self-control task over pet dogs; barn-hunt dogs performed worse in this task.
sources.limits: Cross-sectional training groups (162 dogs) and one laboratory cylinder task; this does not test a leave-it cue or household generalization, and training is not randomized.
sources.use: Caution against claims that generic impulse-control practice transfers broadly.

sources.title: Context specificity of inhibitory control in dogs
sources.author: Bray, MacLean, and Hare
sources.finding: Across three experiments, inhibitory-control scores did not correlate between tasks, indicating strong context/task dependence.
sources.limits: Thirty dogs across three laboratory tasks; cognitive inhibition proxies do not directly measure everyday behavior or compare leave-it protocols.
sources.use: Support cautious, context-specific generalization and avoid framing inhibition as a unitary learned trait.

sources.title: Measures of Dogs’ Inhibitory Control Abilities Do Not Correlate across Tasks
sources.author: Brucks, Marshall-Pescini, Wallis, Huber, and Range
sources.finding: Performance across several inhibitory-control tasks did not show consistent cross-task correlation.
sources.limits: 67 dogs were tested, with varying numbers completing each task; laboratory inhibition proxies do not directly measure everyday behavior or cue generalization.
sources.use: Second independent context-specificity source; contrast with training-specific discrimination research.

sources.title: The effects of cue modality on reliability and generalization of training outcomes with domestic dog
sources.author: Molly A. B. Anderson, Devon K. Otero, Pepe Peruyero, and Nicole R. Dorey
sources.finding: Nine naive pet dogs were studied in two cue-modality experiments. Overall response comparisons were nonsignificant, while combined cues required fewer trials to generalization criterion in the tested novel conditions.
sources.limits: Small, specific cue-training study. Full methods inaccessible; the archive’s same-room detail is not independently confirmed here. Not a leave-it protocol comparison.
sources.use: Relevant evidence that compound cues may aid some transfer, while underscoring that the effect is task- and context-specific.

sources.title: Owner-implemented paired-stimulus food preference assessments for companion dogs
sources.author: Waite and Kodak
sources.type: Methods study of owner-run preference assessment
sources.finding: Owners could implement a paired-food preference protocol with high integrity, and the assessment identified individual preference rankings.
sources.limits: Food preference ranking does not guarantee a food will reinforce every behavior under all conditions; the method was not a general reward test for all reinforcer types.
sources.use: Let owners identify suitable food rewards through safe, simple choice tests.

intro.title: Decide when to advance
intro.body: Use the Move on when section for that exact step. Ordinary skills often use 4 successes in 5 opportunities across two short sessions. That is a practical rule chosen for clarity, not a validated scientific cutoff. Anxiety stages also require comfortable behavior and recovery; obedience or food-taking alone is insufficient.

intro.title: Use short sessions
intro.body: Start with a handful of easy repetitions or roughly 1–3 minutes, then stop or rest. This is a practical starting point, not a research-proven ideal duration. Pick one useful lesson and one enjoyable activity. Keep rewards suitable and account for food used in the daily diet. Do not withhold food, contact, or relief to force participation. Reward each terminal marker promptly, even if you marked an unintended action. Do not require another behavior to earn that promised reward.

intro.title: Keep contexts separate
intro.body: Foundations covers learning the action in a quiet setting. Practice elsewhere covers transfer to specified rooms, outdoors, or mild distractions. A dog can know their name while struggling near another dog; those are different learning goals. Record the actual setting rather than claiming a skill works everywhere. Reward useful offered choices in the situations where you want them, as well as teaching cues for communication. Neither implies a behavior will hold in new settings or when nobody is present; use barriers and secure storage for hazards.

intro.title: Change feelings
intro.body: For classical counterconditioning, a manageable trigger appears or sounds first; desirable food/play follows promptly. No sit, silence, or eye contact is required. For an action such as a head turn or target, reward the action as described. Keep these goals distinct. Do not repeat an overwhelming exposure while waiting for quiet.

intro.title: Know when to simplify
intro.body: Tension, sticky staring, freezing, repeated avoidance, frantic movement, barking/lunging, or slower recovery mean create space, reduce sound/movement, or end the session. Reward or reassure if welcome while helping the dog feel safe. Compare several signs with your dog’s normal baseline; a wagging tail or accepting food does not establish comfort.

intro.title: Get individual support
intro.body: A bite or attempted bite, redirection toward the handler, severe panic, no comfortable starting setup, sudden worsening, or pain signs calls for an individualized plan. A veterinarian can assess health and medication needs; a veterinary behaviorist or experienced reward-based behavior consultant can help. Use barriers and safe distance while arranging help. No dosing advice is provided here.

intro.title: The individual in front of you
intro.body: Tailor practice to your dog’s observed behavior, health, preferences, and handling needs. Choose secure, comfortable equipment that fits this dog. Adjust the setting and rewards to what helps them feel safe and enjoy learning. No breed label determines an individual dog’s needs or justifies harsher methods.

intro.title: Optional advanced jobs
intro.body: Multi-stage jobs are optional supervised enrichment. Use empty safe carriers, low open shelves and lightweight purpose-built training doors. Refrigerators and other food or electrical appliances are excluded from current lessons. Put props and handles away afterward; a simple human-presented retrieve is equally valid.

intro.title: After a difficult day
intro.body: Several close-together challenges can leave a dog less able to cope. Offer predictable rest, space, and enjoyable low-demand activities. Return to planned exposure only when this dog is back at their ordinary comfortable baseline; there is no universal number of hours that certifies recovery.

intro.title: Tricks are optional
intro.body: Choose movements and materials that suit this dog. Use a non-slip surface, safe oversized props, and brief supervised sessions. Stop at stiffness, avoidance, strain, guarding, or frustration. Food puzzles, targets, and household jobs are enrichment, not a substitute for an anxiety treatment plan. Skip anything the dog does not enjoy.

intro.title: Choice during care
intro.body: A chin rest or start posture is only a trained signal. Watch the whole dog and stop hands and tools for withdrawal, freezing, tension or avoidance, even if the posture remains. Resume only after a comfortable voluntary new start. Agree on the stop signal with anyone helping. Necessary or urgent treatment needs a veterinary handling, pain-relief and medication plan; never delay care to finish an app lesson.

evidence.conclusion: Use reward-based teaching, environmental management, and gradual comfortable exposure. Avoid fear, pain, intimidation, forced contact, and flooding.
evidence.limits: Current veterinary behavior guidance supports this approach. Comparative welfare evidence is meaningful, but not every efficacy comparison favors rewards and many designs have limitations. The AVSAB board reaffirmed its 2021 position in 2025.

evidence.conclusion: Let a manageable trigger predict food or enjoyable activity without requiring obedience first. Teach targets, stationing, and disengagement as separate useful actions.
evidence.limits: A 2024 systematic review found promising outcomes across heterogeneous reports, with small samples and inconsistent methods. Its abstract was reviewed; full-text access was unavailable.

evidence.conclusion: Use individually comfortable distance, choice, controlled helpers, and easy retreat. A practical goal is coexistence without greeting.
evidence.limits: Professional guidance supports this framework. No large trial identified here establishes one named observation game as best for every dog, or a breed-specific anxiety protocol.

evidence.conclusion: Teach a comfortable knock response, a mat action, their chain, and visitor presence in separate lessons.
evidence.limits: A small door-arrival study supports detailed component teaching. Its specific device/protocol and limited samples do not establish a cure for severe visitor fear.

evidence.conclusion: Use controlled faint-sound practice separately from plans for unavoidable storms or fireworks. Support comfortable hiding and reassurance when sought.
evidence.limits: An evidence review and caregiver survey support several approaches, but survey success percentages are not randomized effects. Recordings may omit meaningful real-event features. Older reassurance restrictions are not adopted.

evidence.conclusion: Consider health contributions and individualized veterinary care when distress is severe, onset is sudden, or training cannot be kept comfortable.
evidence.limits: A small pain/noise clinical study supports assessment, not the claim all fear is pain. Specific placebo-controlled noise-medication studies justify a vet conversation, not a prescription from this workbook.

evidence.conclusion: No supplement purchase is required. Use an individualized plan instead of relying on product marketing.
evidence.limits: A recent CBD crossover trial did not show anxiety benefit over placebo in its measured population. The result is formulation/context-specific. A new single case combining several treatments cannot prove comparative superiority.

evidence.conclusion: Choose equipment, rewards, practice conditions, and professional support for the individual dog, using their observed preferences, health, and comfort.
evidence.limits: Large survey/genomic work shows substantial individual variation; breed-associated tendencies and genetics can still matter. The review did not identify a breed-specific anxiety-treatment trial. Breed is not an individual risk diagnosis.

evidence.conclusion: A soft marker may help timing; it is optional. Use brief enjoyable sessions and rest. Parallel work is offered for compatible components.
evidence.limits: Simple-task experiments and a complex detection study have different findings on marker benefits. Scheduling studies are small/specific; no universal ideal session length or superior mixed-practice schedule is established.

evidence.conclusion: Look for soft voluntary rest and honor withdrawal during handling. A chin rest or down-stay is not by itself evidence of calm.
evidence.limits: A trained down or chin rest does not demonstrate a relaxed emotional state or guarantee control. Small short veterinary-fear and cooperative-care studies found limited or mixed effects; the cooperative-care study did not consistently honor the trained stop during examinations. These results neither guarantee nor disprove benefits from properly implemented individual care plans.

evidence.conclusion: Choose searches, play, tricks, and household jobs that the dog enjoys. Teach component actions before joining a chain.
evidence.limits: Nosework findings concern a small welfare-proxy experiment, not an anxiety cure. Retrieval and training-prop chains here are original practical adaptations, not validated service-dog protocols. Current lessons exclude refrigerators and other appliances.

evidence.conclusion: The row’s criterion is the guide to advancement. Comfort overrides the availability formula and any success percentage.
evidence.limits: Numbers of repetitions, example durations and two-session checks are adjustable editorial practice targets, not research-validated mastery tests or clinical measures. Several errors, tension or slower recovery mean simplify sooner; never drill to meet a quota. A grade covers the observed step and setting only.

evidence.conclusion: Study protocols without results are not outcome evidence. Access limits, conflicts, and external validity matter.
evidence.limits: The register identifies whether abstract, selected full text or guidance was checked. Protocol R23 is not outcome evidence. Conflicting legacy recommendations and unsupported generalizations are not adopted. The Dogs Trust A03 game uses spoken words, gestures and location; it does not isolate reading or visual-word recognition.

evidence.conclusion: Practice dates show recorded activity. A missing log is not evidence that a dog has forgotten a skill. Short, rewarding refreshers can be useful when the dog is comfortable.
evidence.limits: The default seven-day reminder is a product choice, not a research-established retention threshold. Controlled studies differ by task and population. Set a different interval or turn reminders off. Fear and exposure programs are not automatically scheduled.

evidence.conclusion: Use the owner’s observations to offer a quieter setting, more choice around novelty, or voluntary handling starts. Breed selection alone changes nothing.
evidence.limits: Only four survey-supported breed/trait pairs invite questions. These are not diagnoses or validated treatment algorithms. Adjustments do not lower comfort requirements, automatically complete steps, or prescribe additional repetitions, nutrition or medication.

evidence.conclusion: Treat toy names and picture cues as enjoyable optional experiments. Swap object sides and keep body language neutral. A reliable targeting or retrieve game is valuable even without label discrimination.
evidence.limits: Typical-dog and exceptional word-learner studies do not guarantee vocabulary, rapid learning or an intelligence ranking. For picture cues, keep the target hand and other prompts equally available in both conditions; a gesture-driven response does not establish visual discrimination.

evidence.conclusion: Use light, safe props and comfortable floor-level movement. Build component actions, then combine them into small household jobs.
evidence.limits: These lesson sequences are original practical adaptations. Professional guides support targeting and shaping principles; no study establishes each sequence as an anxiety intervention or an exercise prescription.

evidence.conclusion: Build voluntary mouth-care participation in very small pieces. Use pet-safe materials and obtain a veterinary demonstration.
evidence.limits: A training guide cannot diagnose oral pain, replace dental treatment, or determine which individual dog can safely have their mouth handled. Do not restrain, force the jaw, or use human toothpaste.

evidence.conclusion: Teach useful cues and reinforce useful offered behavior in specific contexts. Practice transfer in easy increments and keep hazards physically inaccessible, especially without supervision.
evidence.limits: Laboratory inhibition tasks often show weak cross-task agreement. They do not compare default versus cued leave-it, establish one global self-control ability, or show that training cannot generalize. Small cue studies do not justify an absent-handler safety guarantee.

evidence.conclusion: Describe the taught task precisely: one familiar odor versus a blank, finding a container, following an easy route, or performing an indication. Control unintended helper and handling cues.
evidence.limits: One target versus a blank is not generalized matching to a reference odor. Fresh samples and container positions can change performance. Specialized detection research informs caution but does not validate these home games or identify which cues guided a dog on a route.

evidence.conclusion: Choose rewards the individual dog wants, keep food appropriate to their diet and deliver a promised marker reward promptly. Do not withhold meals, comfort or relief to obtain participation.
evidence.limits: Preference can vary with context and does not establish a universal reward ranking. Markers are optional tools; observed improvements in a particular task do not establish universal superiority over well-timed food.

stepReasons.LEAVE-1: Keep the first offered disengagement easy; prevent frustration and avoid implying that staring must continue until a cue.
stepReasons.LEAVE-2: A cue can be useful without claiming unsupervised protection. The old title contradicted the protected setup.
stepReasons.LEAVE-3: New context transfer needs its own record; it is not implied by learning the spoken cue.
stepReasons.LEAVE-4: Handler-distance transfer is new learning. No absent-handler or household-wide safety claim is made.
stepReasons.WAIT-1: Offered doorway pauses are compatible with a release cue; reinforcement can include access through a safe interior doorway.
stepReasons.WAIT-2: Door movement, waiting time and context are separate difficulty dimensions.
stepReasons.CROSS-1: Indoor route rehearsal needs the flat-line pause, not completed exposure at a real curb.
stepReasons.CROSS-2: Real crossing adds the actual curb context only when that context is introduced.
stepReasons.ALONE-3: Departure actions can be conditioned independently; they must not be gated behind out-of-view absences or treated as proof of absence tolerance.
stepReasons.OBJECT-1: Counterconditioning does not require approach, calm exploration or obedience before food.
stepReasons.OBJECT-3: Sound conditioning can begin independently of visible movement; combinations require both components to be comfortable.
stepReasons.VISITOR-4: An optional view must not become a gate for nonvisual visitor practice.
stepReasons.STORM-2: A support plan can be ready before an unavoidable event occurs. Completion must not require manufactured exposure or imply a cure.
stepReasons.DOG-1: Assessment should not withhold support until a later lesson.
stepReasons.PARALLEL-1: Maintain trigger-food pairing during comfortable movement; check-ins are separately reinforced rather than a condition of support.
stepReasons.PULL-1: A terminal marker promises prompt reward without an extra release command as a hidden requirement.
stepReasons.PULL-2: Do not mark the pull and then require another response before delivering the promised reward.
stepReasons.POUCH-1: Mark the end of the hold-and-give sequence rather than marking a hold then delaying reward for another required action.
stepReasons.POSE-2: The photograph precedes the terminal marker so continued stillness is not required after a promised reward.
stepReasons.TAKE-1: Reinforce one small criterion at a time and reset only after voluntary release or trade; avoid taking objects forcibly.
stepReasons.TAKE-2: A grip marker earns prompt reward; release to eat is accepted without an additional obedience demand.
stepReasons.KEEP-1: A refresher does not justify promoting every stage or broader context without observing its criterion.
stepReasons.FOODWAIT-1: Bowl manners are optional; essential nutrition and guarding treatment must not depend on compliance.
stepReasons.CARDS-1: Hold the target hand and posture constant across both symbols; otherwise hand presentation can be the actual cue.
stepReasons.CARDS-2: The nose-touch opportunity must be available in both conditions, not only when the stripe card appears.
stepReasons.CARDS-3: Only transfer from the old action cues under comparable conditions supports a visual-discrimination interpretation.
stepReasons.SCENTMATCH-2: A nominal blank is not odorless. Match materials and handling and avoid food or helper cues.
stepReasons.SCENTMATCH-3: One learned target versus a blank is discrimination, not generalized matching-to-sample; remove the misleading reference-sample procedure.
stepReasons.TRACKPERSON-2: Offering a sample does not teach its meaning. Route following can use visual, ground-disturbance or airborne cues.
stepReasons.TRACKPERSON-3: Keep recreational route following distinct from person-specific operational scent tracking.
